scored.body: Apple CEO Tim Cook is stepping down, with the company announcing on Monday that John Ternus will take his place as the head of the technology giant.Cook will become the executive chairman of Apple’s board of directors, the company said. Ternus will officially become CEO on Sept. 1."It has been the greatest privilege of my life to be the CEO of Apple and to have been trusted to lead such an extraordinary company," Cook said in a statement on Monday.John Ternus, senior vice president of hardware engineering at Apple Inc., during an Apple event in New York City, March 4, 2026.Adam Gray/Bloomberg via Getty Images"John Ternus has the mind of an engineer, the soul of an innovator, and the heart to lead with integrity and with honor. He is a visionary whose contributions to Apple over 25 years are already too numerous to count, and he is without question the right person to lead Apple into the future," Cook added.Cook has served as ​Apple's CEO ​since ⁠2011. The company said that under his leadership, Apple has grown from a market capitalization of approximately $350 billion to $4 trillion.Apple CEO Tim Cook speaks during the keynote address at an Apple special event, September 9, 2025 in Cupertino, Calif.Justin Sullivan/Getty ImagesTernus has worked at Apple since 2001 and became a vice president of Hardware Engineering in 2013, according to the company. He has worked on several product lines, including the iPad, AirPods, and Apple Watch.“I am profoundly grateful for this opportunity to carry Apple’s mission forward," Ternus said. He worked under Steve Jobs and referred to Cook as his mentor."I am filled with optimism about what we can achieve in the years to come, and I am so happy to know that the most talented people on earth are here at Apple, determined to be part of something bigger than any one of us," he said.Last month, Cook sat down with "Good Morning America" co-anchor Michael Strahan ahead of the company's milestone 50th anniversary.Popular Reads"What a reflection," Cook said of Apple's longevity.When asked about Apple's biggest contributions over the past five decades, Cook pointed to innovation across industries."You know, you can focus on the product moments, reinventing music, reinventing the smartphone, bringing the creative arts to the table, the creative graphics. Saving people's lives with the watch," he said.At the time, Cook dismissed speculation about stepping down, noting, "I love what I do deeply.""Twenty-eight years ago, I walked into Apple and I've loved every day of it since," he said. "We've had ups and downs, but the people I work with are so amazing. They bring out the best in me. And hopefully, I can bring out the best in them. And Michael, I can't imagine life without Apple."

scored.body: Federal Competition and Consumer Protection Commission (FCCPC) has proposed rules that would place businesses using artificial intelligence (AI) in their marketing under tighter regulation, with fines of up to N100 million for breaches.Federal Competition and Consumer Protection Commission (FCCPC) has proposed rules that would place businesses using artificial intelligence (AI) in their marketing under tighter regulation, with fines of up to N100 million for breaches.The proposal is contained in the draft Sales Promotion Regulations, 2026, which the commission released on September 30, 2026.Under the draft, any business that uses AI, machine learning or other automated technologies for sales promotions, marketing communications or consumer engagement aimed at Nigerian consumers would have to register that use with the commission.The draft creates a section on “Artificial Intelligence and Automated Marketing”. It says content generated by AI or automated systems must be clearly identified as such. It also covers AI chatbots, virtual influencers and automated messaging systems.The proposed rules say the use of these tools must be transparent. They must not involve manipulation, misinformation or the exploitation of consumers’ data or behavioural tendencies. Businesses would also have to let consumers opt out of automated or AI-driven marketing messages.On sanctions, the draft said a corporate body that breaches the regulations could face an administrative penalty of up to N100 million, or 1 per cent of its turnover in the previous year, whichever is higher.A natural person who contravenes the regulations could be fined up to N50 million.The draft also provides that directors of an erring company may be proceeded against, and that such action may include disqualification from serving as a director for up to five years.Separate penalties of up to N10 million are proposed for specific offences. These include failing to award a promised prize, failing to comply with the terms of a promotion, and making a false statement in an application or undertaking.The draft makes businesses responsible for the messages, claims and representations produced by the AI or automated systems they deploy. It adds that liability would arise where such a system produces misleading, discriminatory or harmful promotional outcomes.This means a company could not avoid blame for a misleading promotion by pointing to an automated tool as the source.

articles.headline: I turned Gemini Notebook into my gardening expert; my plants finally stopped dying - Android Police
articles.body: I turned Gemini Notebook into my gardening expert; my plants finally stopped dying    Android Police

scored.body:
Credit: Lucas Gouveia / Android Police | PhotoLife_Style / Shutterstock

Published Oct 4, 2026, 6:00 PM EDT

Khumail has been writing about tech, gadgets and games for almost a decade. You can find his work on international print magazines like Stuff and What Hi-Fi, and even on websites like 91mobiles. He built his first gaming PC at the age of 16 by watching YouTube videos and troubleshooting thanks to Reddit. He's been writing smartphone reviews since 2016, along with PC, games, TVs, audio hardware and motorcycle reviews. He has a bachelor's degree in management with a major in marketing which helped him organise and host What Hi-Fi shows for audiophiles to experience luxury home entertainment systems.

Sign in to your Android Police account

My knowledge of plants and rocket engineering is on the same level. I know nothing about either. So, instead of learning about plants (and soon rocket ships) from Google, I turned the learning exercise into an interactive session with Gemini Notebook. Ideally, I would create a Gemini Gem for this problem, but Gemini Notebook is more interactive and always evolving with new sources and information. It can be a sandboxed AI for anything. It changed the how I collect and use information.

Plant a garden

How to set up a Gemini Notebook as a gardening expert

After I finished charting my expenses, side hustles, and fantasy football team, I looked at how Gemini Notebook could take more things off my plate. Gemini Notebook will not magically fix my plants, but now I can monitor their health and take necessary precautions based on their type and breed. I took photos of my plants from my Google Pixel 11 and uploaded them to a Gemini Notebook. I made sure the plants were photographed during the day and that their specific traits were clearly visible in the photo. This way I don't have to download unnecessary Android apps to track my plants. After Gemini recognized my plants and tagged their type and species, I prompted Gemini to do deep research on them. This lets my Gemini Notebook gather all the crucial information for my plants in one place and store it as a Notebook source. I did this to reduce AI hallucination and context drift. My Gemini Notebook will refer to these researched websites and studies as a source in the future. However, I suggest you read through the sources at least once to cross-check the website's authenticity and data. After vetting the information, I was more confident about my Gemini Notebook's answers.

Watering the context

Double down on the research

Gemini pulls world knowledge that can be a bit ambiguous, and you need to fine-tune this sandbox experience to your home and environment. I would suggest letting Gemini track the weather in your location. This lets the AI understand your region's general climate conditions and suggest changes accordingly. I live in a tropical climate with 60% or more humidity. The soil here tends to dry out quickly, so I have always watered my plants more than usual. However, my Notebook told me that overwatering can lead to root rot in certain plants. It's an obvious answer, but I also take photos of any unnatural plant behavior.

Currently, my Caladium (Caladium bicolor) is drooping and not standing firm. Gemini initially thought it was hibernation season, but told me to check the roots for rot. I told my AI gardener the soil had become soggy, and it immediately told me to drain out excess water and create holes at the bottom for water drainage. This simple fix was a good start to testing my new AI gardener. If you have a lot of indoor plants, I would suggest giving the Notebook context of the room temperature and its position relative to direct sunlight. My Swiss Cheese Vine (Monstera adansonii) was getting black margins with yellow halos. Gemini Notebook quickly identified the lack of humidity in my room due to the air conditioner. These smaller fixes have helped me take care of my plants, and I can do all of this in a single chat without running to Google.

It's a task

Integrate Google Tasks with this

After you set up your AI gardener to your preferences, you still need to make sure your plants can survive the week.

I am bad at watering my plants on time and also changing their soil and position in the sunlight. So I asked my Gemini Notebook to create a weekly task list to keep my plants healthy. It also made a list of monthly tasks that included soil change and fertilizing. I wish Gemini Notebook had an automated way to create a list of tasks in the Google Tasks app, but it doesn't, so you will have to add daily and weekly tasks manually. Strangely enough, you can give Gemini access to your Google Workspace, which includes Google Tasks but not Gemini Notebook. Since you're doing this manually and only once, it will work with any reminder app you choose. Since Gemini Notebook already knows your home environment, you can add photos of any new plants you want to add, and it will tell you whether the plant is suited for your home. Setting up a Gemini Notebook as a gardening expert gives me more confidence when I head to a plant nursery to pick new plants for my home.

Bryan Wolfe has spent 15+ years writing about the tech people actually use — and occasionally the tech they probably shouldn't. With bylines at Yahoo, MakeUseOf, TechRadar, and Digital Trends, he brings an MBA-sharpened perspective to consumer tech, AI tools, and digital productivity. He's based in State College, PA, where he also runs GoingSolo.Life, a solo travel brand for the independently minded.

For several months, I’ve run a travel blogging site, GoingSolo.Life. The site matches solo travelers with city itineraries. I recently started working on an app for the site for both Android and iOS. For the former, I decided to use AI to get the job done since I wasn't interested in learning Kotlin. So I set up a test. I wrote one prompt describing the Android app I envisioned, pasted it into Claude Code, OpenAI's mostly good Codex, and Google's Antigravity, and told each one to build the app and install it on my Google Pixel with no help from me. My guess going in was that at least one would stall on a build error and need rescuing. All three finished the job. The apps they produced are close to interchangeable, and what separated the tools was how long each took and how often it stopped to ask me something.

The app I asked them to build

Travel the world, one tap at a time

Credit: Bryan M. Wolfe / MakeUseOf

One big part of GoingSolo.Life is a cruise hub where you can locate sailing directories, cruise finders, and Facebook community listings for 11 cruise lines. I used that page as the blueprint. The app, which I called Solo at Sea, covers three of those lines: Royal Caribbean, Celebrity, and Viking. Each line gets a Sailings tab with filterable cards and a Communities tab listing Facebook groups. Tapping a card opens the cruise line's website or a Facebook search in the browser. The prompt spelled out the rest. It asked for Kotlin with Jetpack Compose, bundled sample data instead of live scraping, and the site's navy, gold, rust, and cream color scheme. It also set a clear finish line: build the app, install it over USB, and launch it on my Google Pixel 9 Pro XL and the latest version of Android 17. My rules were simple. Every tool got the same prompt, word for word. I could approve permission requests, but I couldn't write code, paste in error messages, or send follow-up instructions.

Claude Code

I ran Claude Code on my Claude Pro subscription with Anthropic's Opus 5.5 model. It finished in just under nine minutes, the fastest of the three. What surprised me was how rarely it needed me. Claude Code asked for permission about three times during the build, and each request was a simple yes-or-no about file and folder permissions. The rest of the time, I just watched it work. It was also the only one that left the last step to me. When Claude Code reported the app was installed, nothing had opened on my phone, so I found Solo at Sea in the app drawer myself. After that, everything checked out. All three cruise lines showed up on the home screen, both tabs loaded, the filters narrowed the list, and every card I tapped opened the browser.

Codex

For Codex, I used my ChatGPT Plus account with GPT-6 -Astgra. The build took just over 14 minutes. Codex asked for permission roughly 10 times. That's part of how Codex works. It runs commands inside a sandbox and asks before stepping outside it, and building an Android app means stepping outside a lot, whether to download build tools or talk to a phone over USB. When it finished, Solo at Sea was already open on my phone. It passed every check the Claude Code version did.

Antigravity

Antigravity is a full code editor, not a terminal tool. I ran it on my Gemini Pro subscription with Gemini 3.8 Flash. It took just over 22 minutes, more than twice as long as Claude Code. It also asked for permission about 30 times, and some of that is on me. To keep things even with the other two, I set Antigravity to Request Review, a mode that asks before every terminal command. By default, many of those commands would have run in a sandbox without asking. I also used Gemini's Flash model, a lighter and faster tier than Claude’s Opus 5.5. Even so, the app opened on my phone automatically and worked just like the other two.

So which one should you use?

Put the three apps side by side, and you'd have a hard time telling who built which. Though the card layouts differed slightly, they all used the same fonts, and the tabs were strikingly similar.

Looking back at the prompt, that makes sense. It named the screens, the fields on every card, the colors, and the framework, so the agents had very few decisions left to make on their own. A looser prompt might have produced three very different apps. Judged only by the finished app, none of them wins. Pay for any of the three, and you can describe an Android app in plain English, then watch it open on your phone in less than half an hour. The difference is in getting there. Claude Code finished first and barely needed me, and it's what I'll open next time I want to paste a prompt and refill my coffee. Codex took about five minutes longer and asked a handful more questions. Antigravity was slowest by a wide margin and asked for approval the most, though part of that comes from the setting I chose. I've written plenty about apps over the years, but I have never built one. This week I built three, each on a lunch break, without writing a single line of Kotlin. Whatever tool you already pay for can do the same for you. In some cases, you can even create the app using a free AI account. Here's another take on creating an app with AI, this time only with a screenshot.

I used AI to track my job rejections. It changed my search, and I got hired.

As told to

Tim Paradis

In her job search, Margareth Felicia Gono created an AI workflow that helped her evaluate roles and analyze interview sentiment

Courtesy of Margareth Felicia Gono

Margareth Felicia Gono, 24, recently started as a senior associate at DoorDash after completing a master's degree in applied analytics in May. During her job search, she created an AI workflow that helped her evaluate roles and analyze interview sentiment. The following is based on conversations that have been edited for brevity and clarity.At the beginning of my job search, it was pretty scattershot. Because I was an international student and needed a visa, I felt I had to apply to anything that might relate to my experience, even if it wasn't the right fit.I grew up in Indonesia and didn't want to leave the US without getting corporate experience. My parents paid for my tuition at a private university, then an Ivy League master's on top of that.I started tracking my results. What roles got responses? What didn't? What patterns showed up? Anxiety is unprocessed data. I was tired of feeling bad about my search and figured I might as well learn something instead.Around the second or third round of interviews, I noticed I would get a little bit of hesitation from employers, and I wanted to understand why that was happening. Was it me, my experience, my résumé, or that I needed a visa?I used Claude as a career coachI used Claude almost like a partner and built this tracker for my applications. I'd take a job description and ask Claude to identify the main skills, keywords, and themes. Then I built another automation agent into that same project. Basically, it was my own version of what people call an ATS score. I'd paste the job description and my résumé together and ask, "What top keywords am I missing?"I didn't want AI to invent experience or make me sound like everyone else. I wanted it to show me where my experience wasn't being communicated clearly enough. Sometimes that meant changing one bullet. Sometimes it meant realizing that applying would be a waste of time.As I went along, I became more intentional about who I wanted to work under and what types of jobs I applied for. I used Claude to act like a career coach and figured out I liked three things: talking to people, making things pretty, and finding patterns. As a result, I made three résumés: one for analytics, one for sales and marketing, and one for consulting.Eventually, I used Claude to turn that into a simple dashboard, so I could see what was happening: 186 applications, 44 cold outreaches, 19 interviews, six take-home assignments, three final rounds, and one offer. Seeing it that way made the process feel less like 185 personal failures, and more like a funnel I could keep improving.

I treated an interview like a conversationDuring the process, I started treating every interview like a real conversation instead of an audition. I also really wanted to find someone who was not just a good boss but also a good mentor.When recruiters said they were using an AI note-taker, I'd ask if I could record, too. Most said no. With the yeses, I would scrape the notes and use a sentiment analysis to figure out where I hesitated or used filler words, where the interviewer asked me to get more specific, where they seemed engaged, agreed, or laughed. Even when I couldn't record, I'd write down what I remembered right after — what they asked, where I rambled, what seemed to interest them.I also used AI to research the people I was interviewing with. I built a skill in Claude to scrape LinkedIn profiles. I copy and paste everything on their page, and by now, Claude knows who I am because I talk to it a lot. So I ask it to find similarities to me. In one case, I connected with a recruiter over a cheese club we'd both been part of, years apart. That got me further than any cover letter or résumé font choice ever did.I also think the questions at the end of an interview can make or break it. I would ask how they got to where they are, and what advice they'd give someone just graduating. I think when you stop letting the interviewer drive the entire conversation and actually engage back, you go further.It's easy to have imposter syndrome, but I tried to remember that this is a process, and I know my experience. I've done my research. I know why I want to apply to this job, and if they don't see my value, someone else will.Everyone has access to AI now, so that isn't a differentiator. What makes the difference is knowing what to ask, how to interpret what AI gives you, and where judgment still matters. AI can help you see patterns, but you have to decide what they mean. It can help you get your foot in the door, but it can't make you want the job or make someone remember you.Do you have a story to share about your job search? Contact this reporter at tparadis@businessinsider.com.

articles.headline: I replaced ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, and Perplexity with free open-source alternatives - XDA
articles.body: I replaced ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, and Perplexity with free open-source alternatives    XDA

scored.body:
Published Oct 3, 2026, 5:30 PM EDT

Mahnoor Faisal is a tech journalist covering AI and productivity tools with bylines at XDA, SlashGear, MakeUseOf, Laptop Mag, and Android Police.

She's been writing professionally since she was sixteen, and has since penned hundreds of articles. This includes in-depth coverage of AI tools like NotebookLM to breaking news across the AI space. Her passion for technology started when she received her first iPod Touch (4th generation) on her 8th birthday, and she's been deep in the tech world ever since.

Currently pursuing a degree in computer science, Mahnoor brings both a journalist's eye and a technical foundation to her coverage of how AI is reshaping the way we work and learn.

Sign in to your XDA account

While my bank already hated to see Apple Music, Spotify, Canva, Adobe Creative Cloud, iCloud+, Google One, Netflix, and about half a dozen other subscriptions coming every month, I know AI tools have made an already existing problem significantly worse. Now, practically every AI tool I use wants its own cut too. Claude Max, ChatGPT Plus, Google AI Pro, Perplexity Pro, Cursor Pro, and so on. Unlike the subscriptions I listed at the very beginning, though, AI subscriptions overlap a lot more. Spotify and Canva are solving completely different problems. ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, Perplexity, and Cursor, on the other hand, can all do many of the same things —they just tend to be better at different parts of the job. That overlap is exactly what made me wonder how many of them I actually needed to be paying for. Instead of looking for one open-source app that could somehow replace everything, I decided to rebuild the different parts of my AI workflow with free, open-source alternatives and see how much I could get away with.

Jan

My local LLM finally feels (well, looks) like ChatGPT

After analyzing the kind of tasks I use AI for, I've realized local LLMs can handle the bulk of my work quite easily. Sure, there are inevitably tasks where I still want the stronger reasoning, larger context windows, or specialized tools that come with frontier models, but most of what I ask AI to do on a normal day really isn't that demanding. While I initially relied on Ollama and LM Studio for all my local AI needs, Jan ended up being a much better fit for what I was actually trying to replace. Ollama primarily positions itself as a way to run and build with open models, while LM Studio focuses on making local AI easy to run on your computer. Jan's pitch is a lot more aligned with what users like me want. It's described outright as an open-source replacement for ChatGPT and Claude. After using it, I can see why. The biggest difference is that Jan doesn't feel like I'm opening an app just to run a local model. It feels like I'm opening an AI assistant. The interface is very ChatGPT-like. I can keep separate conversations and Projects, create custom Assistants with their own instructions, upload files, switch between different models, and connect extra tools through MCP. Getting a model running is also much less intimidating than the phrase "local LLM" makes it sound. Jan has its own model hub connected to Hugging Face, so instead of downloading GGUF files manually and figuring out whether your laptop can actually run them, you can browse models from inside the app. It's also not local-only, and ships with about a dozen of remote providers. This means I can use Jan for both my local and cloud models. What really sold me on it, though, is that going local doesn't automatically mean giving up all the extras I've gotten used to with ChatGPT. Jan has web search and page fetching built in, so supported models can still pull in current information instead of being stuck with whatever they were trained on. And if I want to take things further, MCP lets me add things like browser control and other external tools! Though Ollama is excellent at running models, I've found that Jan is much better at handling everything around them. It feels like a middle ground between Ollama, LM Studio, and Open WebUI!

Vane

Perplexity, minus the Pro plan

Vane, previously known as Perplexica, has long been advertised as an open-source alternative to Perplexity, and I can see why! At its core, Vane is an AI-powered search engine that searches the web, pulls together relevant information, and gives you a summarized answer with sources attached. So, basically, the reason I use Perplexity in the first place. The difference is that Vane can run with local models through Ollama, which means I don't necessarily need to send every question off to another company's servers. It uses SearXNG underneath for web search, and I can choose between different search modes depending on what I'm doing. Speed Mode is there when I just want a quick answer, Balanced Mode is meant for normal searches, and Quality Mode digs deeper when I actually care about the research. I can also narrow searches down to things like the general web, discussions, or academic papers instead of throwing every source type into the same pile. That sounds fairly basic on paper, but it's exactly the kind of stuff that makes Perplexity useful to me. I rarely open it because I want to have a long conversation with an AI. I open it because I want to ask a question, get something reasonably current back, and immediately see where the information came from. Vane supports image and video search, lets me upload files and ask questions about them, can restrict searches to specific domains, and even has widgets for things like weather, calculations, and stock prices! That said, Vane is nowhere near as frictionless as just opening Perplexity.com and using it. You need to go through the hassle of setting it up, and Docker is the recommended route. However, once it's running, I get most of the parts of Perplexity I actually care about without paying for another AI subscription.

Open Design

My second designer doesn’t need a subscription

While a Claude subscription was once limited to the actual Chat panel, it’s since expanded into much more of a full-fledged workspace. You get Claude Code, Cowork, and a relatively newer feature called Claude Design. One of the best use cases I’ve personally found for AI is using it as a secondary designer. I’m not a very creative person, and I spend way more time than I can afford perfecting slide decks, posters, infographics, and even content for socials. That’s why I’ve been experimenting a lot with Claude Design since it launched. It can take a prompt and turn it into things like slides, one-pagers, prototypes, and other polished visual assets. You can then edit them right within the interface using prompts or by tweaking individual elements yourself. This makes it feel a lot less like a one-and-done image generator and more like having a second designer sitting beside you. However, once I tested Open Design, a completely open-source alternative built around the same idea, I never really felt the need to keep paying $20 just for access to something like Claude Design. Open Design is local-first and lets you use the AI agent you already prefer as the actual design engine. That can be Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Gemini CLI, OpenCode, or several others, rather than locking you into Anthropic’s models. It can generate things like websites, prototypes, slides, images, and other visual assets, and the output stays as actual files you can keep working with instead of living inside a closed platform. That flexibility is probably what I like most about it. I can keep the same general prompt-to-design workflow I liked in Claude Design, but I’m not tied to a single model or subscription to do it. If I want to use OpenCode one day and Gemini CLI the next, I can. I can also bring in my own design system through a DESIGN.md file, so the output can follow the same colors, typography, spacing, and overall style instead of starting from scratch every single time.

Open Code

Claude Code and Codex, but I get to pick the model

For the longest time, the only reason I could justify my Claude subscription was Claude Code. I've developed a fairly good system around it at this point, and I use it for everything from fixing tiny bugs to making changes across entire projects. While it's excellent at what it does, the catch is, yet again, that I'm bound to Anthropic's models only. Codex has been my current favorite, but it comes with the exact same problem: I can only use OpenAI's models with it.

Given that different models have different capabilities, I feel like locking an entire coding workflow to one provider is unnecessarily limiting. There are times when Claude is better at understanding a messy codebase, times when an OpenAI model handles a task better, and plenty of smaller jobs where I really don't need to be paying for a frontier model at all. That's exactly where OpenCode comes in. It gives me most of the things I've already built my Claude Code workflow around, including a dedicated planning mode, Skills, MCP server support, and the ability to actually read and make changes across a project. The key difference is that the agent itself isn't tied to one company's models. I can swap between Claude, OpenAI, Gemini, or even local models depending on what I'm working on, without having to rebuild the rest of my setup around them.

Open Notebook

NotebookLM, but I call the shots

As an added bonus, this entire experiment also made me realize there was another AI subscription I probably didn't need to keep around. I've written about NotebookLM far more than any normal person reasonably should, and I still think it's one of the best AI tools Google has made. However, a huge part of why I use it comes down to the features it built around my sources rather than the chatbot itself. Open Notebook gets surprisingly close to replicating that. I can upload my own sources, ask questions grounded in them, generate summaries and notes, and even create NotebookLM-style Audio Overviews from the material I've added. That's easily one of my favorite NotebookLM features, since I can turn a pile of notes, readings, or research into something I can listen to instead of sitting down and going through everything again. Of course, NotebookLM still has more polish and some newer features Open Notebook doesn't completely replicate. But if the main things I want are source-grounded chat, summaries, notes, and Audio Overview-style podcasts, Open Notebook covers a surprisingly large chunk of why I use NotebookLM in the first place.

scored.body:
Following the compute-based usage change in May, Google will soon introduce limits on which Gemini models free users and AI Plus subscribers can access.

According to an updated support document this week, Gemini app users without a Google AI subscription will be limited to the (3.5) Flash-Lite model. Starting October 9, users who do not pay for Gemini will no longer be able to access (3.6) Flash or (3.1) Pro.

Meanwhile, AI Plus subscribers will be limited to Flash-Lite and Flash, with Pro no longer available. These $4.99 per month users will “receive an email that explains when these changes will take effect.”

Gemini ModelGoogle AI PlanFlash-LiteFlashProWithout a plan✓XXAI Plus✓✓XAI Pro✓✓✓AI Ultra✓✓✓

There are no regressions for AI Pro and AI Ultra. Rather, $19.99/month customers will get access to the Deep Think option for “maximum parallel reasoning” that’s currently just on the $99.99 and $199.99/month plans.

Gemini 3.1 Pro with Deep Think on AI Ultra

In October, the Gemini app also looks to be adding new “low,” “medium,” and “high” effort levels “for each available model.”

This will increase the model’s ability to complete tasks and provide more thorough answers to queries, but will also use more of your limit.

At the moment, you can just enable “Extended thinking: Complex problem solving.” The three new effort/thinking levels would match what’s available in Google AI Studio and Antigravity.

It’s not clear where Gemini 4 Argon will fit in. Google announced earlier this week that it’s first coming to AI Ultra subscribers. The company has yet to specify whether Argon will be classified as a Pro model or be part of a new tier above it.

scored.body:
The ruins of NASA's Gemini program: Launch Complex 19

Nestled within “missile row” at the Cape Canaveral Space Force Station rests Launch Complex 19, a remnant of one of NASA’s most ambitious programs: Project Gemini. Gemini served as the bridge between Project Mercury and Project Apollo, completing demanding tasks such as long-duration space missions, rendezvous, docking, extravehicular activities and more. It laid the groundwork for how humans could live and work in space and ensured the possibility of making it to the Moon and back with the Apollo program.Behind every Gemini mission was a launch complex that made the program possible.From Titan I to Titan IIThe U.S. Air Force constructed Launch Complex 19 for the HGM-25A Titan I, an intercontinental ballistic missile, or ICBM. The Titan I was also launched from nearby Launch Complexes 15, 16 and 20.The Titan I was eventually retired in favor of the newer and more powerful Titan II, which shared much of the same lineage as its predecessor. The Titan II could carry a 9 megaton warhead, more than double the payload capacity of the Titan I.

The Titan I missile (left) and the Titan II GLV (right), both launching from Launch Complex 19.

U.S. Air Force / NASA

NASA selected the Titan II as the launch vehicle for Gemini because it could carry the heavier two-person spacecraft into orbit, which the older Atlas rocket used for the Mercury program could not do.The Titan II was given the name Titan II GLV (Gemini Launch Vehicle), designating it as human-rated.The Gemini Program overviewNASA’s Gemini program followed the Mercury program with bigger and bolder goals. First, NASA needed to learn how astronauts could survive long-duration spaceflights, which would be necessary for missions to the Moon and back. Second, astronauts needed to learn how to rendezvous with other spacecraft in orbit. Third, they needed to demonstrate docking, or connecting two spacecraft in space. Finally, NASA needed to determine how astronauts could safely work outside their spacecraft, known as an extravehicular activity, or EVA. The Gemini program accomplished these goals over the course of 12 flights, two uncrewed and 10 crewed.For James Draper, director of the Cape Canaveral Space Force Museum, Launch Complex 19 represents an important chapter in the story of America’s early human spaceflight program.“For us, Launch Complex 19 is a key part of the whole Cape Canaveral Space Force Station narrative. As far as the early manned missions, the Gemini program was really fascinating. You had Mercury getting us to space, Gemini learning how to operate in space and then Apollo taking us to the Moon.”One of the missions that demonstrated Gemini’s importance was Gemini 5, which set an eight-day spaceflight endurance record. Draper pointed to Gemini 5 as one of the significant missions that launched from LC-19, in part because of the artifacts that remain from it today.

Gemini 5 on the launch pad at LC-19. The launch erector is the structure retracting to the left, with the Gemini white room on top. The red structures to the right are the service and umbilical towers.

NASA

“One of the most significant ones would be GT-5, and that’s mainly because we have a tangible connection to it in Hangar C with the GT-5 booster segment. And it’s the only recovered booster from all of Mercury, Gemini and Apollo put together.”He also explained why the mission’s eight-day duration was so important.“And what’s really cool about that mission was the duration in space record that they set of eight days. And why is eight days significant? Well, that’s the period of time you need to travel safely to the Moon and back.”

The GT-5 booster segment at the Hangar C exhibit at the Cape Canaveral Space Force Museum.

Jake Bradshaw

According to NASA, the first American EVA took place on the Gemini 4 mission, performed by Ed White. He spent 23 minutes outside the capsule, using a Hand-Held Maneuvering Unit to propel himself outside while being linked to the spacecraft with a tether. Following Gemini 5, another significant mission was Gemini 8, which achieved the first docking of two spacecraft in orbit but also resulted in an out-of-control spacecraft.To conclude the Gemini program, Gemini 12 was flown by Jim Lovell and Buzz Aldrin, who would later become the second person to walk on the Moon during Apollo 11. They completed three EVAs totaling five hours and 37 minutes, as well as rendezvous and docking with the Agena Target Vehicle and an automated reentry. This was the final launch from Launch Complex 19.Construction and key components of the padAccording to the Cape Canaveral Space Force Museum archives, Launch Complex 19 began construction on February 18, 1957, for the Titan I missile program. The final Titan I launch from LC-19 took place on January 29, 1962, and the pad was turned over for the Gemini Program and the Titan II GLV.The blockhouse, a reinforced-concrete structure housing launch control and mission operators, stood 650 feet away from the launch ramp. The blockhouse had two floors, with the firing room located on the second floor and the instrumentation rooms on the first. Launch operators could view the launch via a periscope or CCTV monitors.

The long abandoned blockhouse left overgrown.

Jake Bradshaw

The entrance to the blockhouse with the blast doors that would have closed the entryway are visible to the left.

Jake Bradshaw

Two blast doors at the entrance to the blockhouse were covered with thick steel plates and were designed to protect personnel from the effects of an explosion at the launch pad. These doors would have been shut prior to any event at the launch pad where an issue could occur, such as a pre-launch rehearsal or an actual launch itself.The Titan rockets used a launch erector to assemble the vehicle horizontally before rotating it vertically for launch. The launch erector also contained the white room at the very top, which was used to mate and assemble the Gemini capsule on top of the Titan II booster. On launch day, the astronauts would ride an elevator up to the white room to complete final suit checks and board the capsule.

A view looking out from the top of the launch ramp. To the left would have been the launch erector with the white room on top, which would have rested in the concrete opening to the far left.

Jake Bradshaw

After the rocket went vertical, it was secured to the thrust mount, which was positioned in front of the concrete launch ramp. Just before launch, the erector would be lowered back down to the horizontal position.Around the corner from the launch ramp sat the oxidizer farm, which stored the nitrogen tetroxide propellant. This oxidizer farm, paired with the fuel farm down the road, which stored Aerozine-50, would fuel the Titan II rocket before launch. Both chemicals would combust spontaneously upon contact, without needing any external ignition source, which allowed for the Titan II to launch within about a minute.The Theodolite Building is situated about 250 feet directly to the right of the launch mount. This building housed specialized optical surveying instruments, which were important to align the rocket vertically on the launch pad and provide precise tracking information.

The Theodolite Building resting in some overgrown tall grass.

Jake Bradshaw

Finally, there was a catch basin used to collect and neutralize hazardous fluids, such as spilled rocket fuel or contaminated water from the deluge system. This would protect toxic chemicals from entering Cape Canaveral’s drainage canals.All of these structures directly supported launch operations for each mission.What’s left behindAs of 2026, not much remains of the original launch site.Left standing are the concrete launch ramp, the blockhouse, the fuel and oxidizer farms, the theodolite building and the catch basin.In 1977, the service and umbilical towers were demolished, leaving the pad erector and white room left to rot away in the Florida humidity until 2003.In 2003, the Space Force Museum acquired the Gemini white room, which underwent restoration and is now on display at the Space Force Museum annex at the Launch Complex 26 blockhouse.After the launch mount and erector were left dormant for more than 30 years, the remaining structures were demolished between 2012 and 2013, leaving behind the concrete launch ramp.Although much of LC-19 has been left to deteriorate, the story of the Gemini program continues to be preserved through artifacts at other locations around Cape Canaveral. Draper explained that the Space Force Museum uses these artifacts to help visitors understand the history of the complex and the program.“Here in the Sands Space History Center, we tell the story of the Cape by launch complex … So, here we’ve got a whole section devoted to Launch Complex 19. We use a Gemini test console that’s been restored to help provide a tangible connection to that past. But, I think we do a better job preserving and telling the story of the Gemini program at our other sites.”Among those sites are the Sands Space History Center, Hangar C and the Launch Complex 26 museum annex, which house several major Gemini artifacts.“At the main museum grounds, the Gemini white room, the largest Gemini program-related artifact in existence. And that’s just a visually appealing piece. Then the second-largest Gemini-related piece in our collection is the GT-5 booster segment at Hangar C, another great visceral connection. And then Gemini 2 in the exhibit hall at Launch Complex 26, America’s first reused spacecraft. I mean, there’s nothing like it out there.”

The concrete launch ramp left behind after demolition of the launch mount, launch erector and service and umbilical towers.

Jake Bradshaw

The Gemini white room on display at the Launch Complex 26 museum annex of the Space Force Museum.

Jake Bradshaw

With the Gemini program complete, LC-19 was no longer needed for future missions. Like many of the launch complexes at Cape Canaveral, the site was abandoned in place rather than being completely dismantled. Draper explained why this became common practice across the Cape.“It should have been right after the end of Project Gemini when it was abandoned in place. Like a lot of these complexes that you see noted around the gallery, once the program ran its course, the complex was abandoned in place and that was just the MO out here. There’s enough land to do that. Everything was kind of proprietary, so you’d have to tear everything up and rebuild to do a new program, and it was just easier to abandon in place.”Future preservationToday, the question is not only what remains of LC-19, but what will happen to the site in the future. Draper explained how the museum currently views the possibility of preserving the complex:“From the museum standpoint? Probably not. But will it be developed for commercial space? In the short term, I don’t see that happening because of nearby operations, keeping it relatively safe from development, Relativity’s (Relativity Space) safety arc extends over that complex. So, the Delta (Space Launch Delta 45) isn’t going to reallocate that to another commercial launch outfit as far as I know, which will help preserve in a way the aerospace ruins that exist there.”“But, the fact that they are ruins doesn’t really help in any potential future restorations. At most, maybe keeping the vegetation at bay and stabilizing in the future. But, the museum doesn’t have any designs to acquire any of those structures just because of their state of decay, their proximity to operations, and all kinds of other things. Now, the future can change on a whim. There’s no telling what will happen … but as of now, Complex 19 still sits, still remains as aerospace ruins, and provides some connection to that 1960s period. The future is unknown for that site.”The rockets are gone, the missions are over and much of Launch Complex 19 has disappeared into the Florida landscape. What remains is more than concrete and abandoned buildings. It is a physical reminder of the Gemini program and the astronauts who helped prove that humans could learn to live and work in space.

articles.body: Anthropic says Claude can work with Android apps now, so I tested it against Gemini    MakeUseOf

scored.body:
Published Oct 3, 2026, 1:30 PM EDT

Abhijith has been writing for the Web since 2011 and has contributed to sites like Beebom and TechWiser. He is curious about making the best of tech accessible to everyone.

He started writing as a hobby after getting a computer at 16. Since then, he has found technical writing a space where he belongs and could make a difference. A curious and self-motivated person, Abhijith's writings focus on productivity, Android, and the Internet.

He holds a Master's degree in English and a PhD in Humanities. Enthusiastic about language, literature, and culture, he works as an Assistant Professor of English.

If not writing or reading, you can find Abhijith playing Chess or CODM.

It's no secret that I love Claude and prefer it to ChatGPT and Gemini! I also reach out to the Claude Android app more often than to Gemini for many tasks. So, you can imagine my excitement when I heard that Claude can now work with Android apps. In a support page published on August 25, the company explained how Claude can access multiple apps/features on an Android smartphone. Surely, I wanted to check out the feature and believed Claude might as well replace Gemini on my device. Last week, I updated Claude for Android to the latest version and decided to test its Android capabilities against Gemini's.

What Claude claims it can control on Android

It's a rather extensive list

Before I tell you what worked and what didn't, we must understand what Anthropic claims Claude can do. According to Anthropic, Claude can help you with the following:

Drafting and sending messages using default messaging apps and third-party ones like WhatsApp and Slack

Composing emails so that the email app will open with the drafted content prefilled

Set alarms and timers using the corresponding apps on Android

Display locations on maps and show navigation options

Access current location and offer contextual suggestions

I was pretty excited to see this new functionality. For what it's worth, Anthropic does mention a few limitations, such as the feature not being able to access contacts, reminders, or calendar events owned by others. It also mentions how some features are limited to certain subscription plans and geographical locations.

The alarm and timer requests never failed

Spoiler: they don't need Gemini's help

There are two actions that Claude could easily perform on my Android smartphone: setting a timer and setting an alarm. The idea is simple: you want to do something within a time, and you ask Claude to set a timer for, let's say, 2 minutes. Within a second, Claude started the timer, and I could see it running in the default Clock app on my smartphone. There was also a See Timers button, but it led me straight to the Clock app, not a Claude page. Similarly, you can set an alarm. You'd say something like, "Set an alarm for 11:30 am," and Claude does the job. This is an area where you see the benefit of AI: if you say a time that could mean two different things, Claude will ask you for clarification. One evening, I asked Claude to set an alarm for 11:00, and the AI chatbot asked me whether I meant 11 am or a few hours after. These options worked well and are pretty well integrated with Android.

Calendar management is the pleasant surprise

Potential conflicts aside, it just scheduled things

Calendar management is one of those areas where Claude for Android makes life easier and efficiently manages your smartphone calendar. As someone who manages multiple calendars on my device, I find it useful to view and manage events from a chatbot I regularly use. Claude seems to deliver on this front.

Note: It's slightly different if you have set up a Google Calendar connection. When you ask for a calendar management system, Claude will resort to that option. To access your device calendar, turn off the Google Calendar connector, so Claude can access it instead.

When you set up calendar access for the first time, you can choose which calendars Claude can access. This is a great option because the Google Calendar connector only allows you to connect one account, but I have multiple accounts on my device. This feature has been pretty useful. Once the setup is done, you can ask Claude to show you what's ahead for you next week or to add a new event. Once again, Claude's smart chatbot can understand when you say something confusing and will give you a couple of options to choose from. Generally, using Claude to manage my calendar has been a pleasant experience, as long as we avoid ownership and other conflicts.

Some features that never quite worked

These sections need serious work before they're advertised

Messaging, maps, and location-based suggestions are a few other things that Anthropic claims Claude can do on Android, but these were better when promised than delivered. Compared to the other options I tested, the features built into Claude for messaging people or getting location-based suggestions were either broken or seemed to need a mediator.

Messaging options heavily relied on web-based connectors

Though Anthropic claims that Claude for Android can send text messages along with WhatsApp and Slack messages, this did not seem to work. Even when I specifically asked Claude to send a message to a given number, it explicitly told me that it cannot send WhatsApp or text messages, but instead opened a link where it loaded WhatsApp.

When I asked Claude to send a message via Slack, it opened the web-based connector I had set up earlier. When I turned off this connector and tried again, Claude asked me to turn it on. Sure, this technically means that Claude can send a message on Slack, but it doesn't do anything specific on an Android smartphone. Instead, it uses a generic connector available on all devices.

When it came to maps and location-based suggestions, Claude did deliver, but it almost felt like the app was simply pulling in content from Google Maps and synthesizing it at a very surface level.

Email and maps-based actions don't work as advertised, either

The situation was somewhat similar when I asked Claude to send an email as well. It immediately resorted to the connected Gmail account and asked if it could do it for me. When I turned off the connector, the option did not exist, and it said it could offer me an “Open in Mail” button, which is half-baked, to say the least. When it came to maps and location-based suggestions, Claude did deliver, but it almost felt like the app was simply pulling in content from Google Maps and synthesizing it at a very surface level. It did not offer the seamless experience I got when I was asking it to check my calendar or set a timer. Similarly, it says it can help you navigate to a location, but it could not start turn-by-turn navigation at all.

Not a Gemini replacement, at least not yet

For all I love what Claude has built for Android, it is not yet a Gemini replacement. As you can clearly see, there are sections that need a revamp and better permissions to offer an experience that matches Gemini's. Given that Anthropic has optimized certain features, such as timers, calendars, and alarms, for a smoother experience, I'm sure there'll be better options. Until then, though, I will stick to Gemini for most of my AI assistance needs and give Claude a try sometime later!

articles.body: GPT-6 Luna vs Sonnet 5.5 vs Grok 4.7: 20x Price Gap [2026]    tech-insider.org

scored.body:
October 5, 2026 21 min read

Three AI labs shipped three different bets inside a single week this past September, and the gap between them says a lot about where the AI model market is actually headed in late 2026. OpenAI pushed out GPT-6 Luna on September 22 as its cheapest workhorse model. Anthropic answered six days later with Claude Sonnet 5.5, a mid-tier model built for speed. xAI, meanwhile, had already shipped Grok 4.7 on September 21, chasing coding and agentic workloads with a tiered pricing structure unlike anything else on the market.What GPT-6 Luna, Claude Sonnet 5.5, and Grok 4.7 Actually AreGPT-6 Luna vs Claude Sonnet 5.5 vs Grok 4.7: Full Specs TablePricing Breakdown: Where Each Model Actually Lands on CostBenchmark Performance: Intelligence, Coding, and Agentic TasksSpeed and Latency: Which Model Responds FastestContext Window and Multimodal Capability ComparedReal-World Use Cases: Where Each Model Actually FitsPros and Cons: GPT-6 LunaPros and Cons: Claude Sonnet 5.5Pros and Cons: Grok 4.7Migration Guide: Switching Between These Three ModelsMoving to GPT-6 Luna for cost savingsMoving to Claude Sonnet 5.5 from Sonnet 5 or Opus-tier modelsMoving to or from Grok 4.7Which Model Should Canadian Businesses Choose in October 2026How These Models Fit Into the Broader September 2026 AI Release WaveWhy This Three-Way Split Reflects a Bigger Shift in the AI MarketIntegration Code Example: Switching Providers With Minimal ReworkData Residency and Enterprise Considerations for Canadian TeamsCommon Mistakes Teams Make Choosing Between These ThreeRate Limits, Availability, and Developer ExperienceFrequently Asked QuestionsIs GPT-6 Luna cheaper than Claude Sonnet 5.5?Which model has the largest context window?Which of these three models scores highest on benchmarks?Is Grok 4.7 good for coding tasks?Does Claude Sonnet 5.5 cost more than Sonnet 5?What happens if a Grok 4.7 prompt goes over 200,000 tokens?Can I use GPT-6 Luna for coding tasks?Are these three models available through cloud providers like AWS or Google Cloud?

For Canadian developers, IT buyers, and businesses choosing an API provider in October 2026, the decision is no longer just “which model is smartest.” It is which model is smart enough, fast enough, and cheap enough for the actual job at hand. GPT-6 Luna, Claude Sonnet 5.5, and Grok 4.7 sit at wildly different points on that curve, and this comparison breaks down the pricing, the benchmark data, and the real trade-offs so you don’t have to run your own burn-rate experiment to find out.

Google · Preferred SourcesDon't miss new tech stories on Google

Add Tech Insider once in the Google app and our stories appear in your news suggestions.

Add Now

What GPT-6 Luna, Claude Sonnet 5.5, and Grok 4.7 Actually Are

GPT-6 Luna is OpenAI’s budget tier inside the GPT-6 family, sitting below GPT-6 Sol and the flagship GPT-6 Astra. OpenAI launched it alongside GPT-6 Sol on September 22, 2026, positioning Luna for “high-volume tasks with a clear goal, like summarizing documents, extracting information, or answering quick questions,” according to TechCrunch’s coverage of the launch. It is not meant to compete with frontier reasoning models. It is meant to make repetitive, high-throughput workloads cheap enough to run at scale without a second thought.

Claude Sonnet 5.5 occupies a different lane entirely. Anthropic’s own product page describes it as the second model in the Claude 5.5 family, arriving after Claude Opus 5.5 and positioned as what the company calls a faster, lower-cost complement to Claude Opus 5.5. Anthropic’s announcement states Sonnet 5.5 runs more than 30 percent faster than Sonnet 5 and costs up to 30 percent less for most workloads, while keeping the same per-token pricing as its predecessor. Sonnet 5.5 is Anthropic’s mid-market answer: not the cheapest model on this list, but the one built to handle serious coding and reasoning work without flagship pricing.

Grok 4.7 is xAI’s play for coding and agentic tasks specifically. According to xAI’s own developer release notes, it ships with a 500,000-token context window, accepts both text and image input but returns text-only output, and supports four reasoning effort levels — low, medium, high, and xhigh — with high set as the default. Its pricing structure is tiered by prompt length, a design choice neither OpenAI nor Anthropic uses for these three models.

The three models were not built to be direct substitutes for each other. That’s precisely why comparing them matters: picking the wrong one for your workload either burns budget on a model more capable than the task requires, or produces a product that quietly underperforms because it was running on a model tuned for keyword summarization rather than agentic reasoning.

GPT-6 Luna vs Claude Sonnet 5.5 vs Grok 4.7: Full Specs Table

Here is the complete technical breakdown, pulled from each company’s own documentation and release notes as of early October 2026.

SpecGPT-6 LunaClaude Sonnet 5.5Grok 4.7

DeveloperOpenAIAnthropicxAI (SpaceXAI)

Release dateSeptember 22, 2026September 28, 2026September 21, 2026

Input pricing (per 1M tokens)$0.10$2.00$2.00 (≤200K prompt) / $4.00 (>200K prompt)

Output pricing (per 1M tokens)$0.50$10.00$6.00 (≤200K prompt) / $12.00 (>200K prompt)
