PositioningHigh-volume, low-cost clerical and automation workMid-tier flagship complement — coding, reasoning, agentic workCoding and agentic tasks with adjustable reasoning depth

Price cut vs predecessor50% cheaper input, 58.3% cheaper output vs GPT-5.6 LunaSame sticker price as Sonnet 5, but 30%+ faster and up to 30% cheaper effective costNot directly comparable — first model in this exact pricing structure

A few things jump out immediately. GPT-6 Luna’s context window is technically the largest of the three at 1,050,000 tokens, but its Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index score of 38.1 places it well below both Sonnet 5.5 and Grok 4.7 on raw reasoning capability — the trade-off OpenAI designed intentionally. Claude Sonnet 5.5’s climb to #2 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index v4.3.2, trailing only its own sibling Claude Opus 5.5 (which scores 58), is the single most notable benchmark result among the three.

Pricing Breakdown: Where Each Model Actually Lands on Cost

Price is the dimension that separates these three the most sharply, and it’s worth laying out in Canadian-dollar terms since none of these companies bill natively in CAD. At an approximate exchange rate of 1 USD to 1.38 CAD as of early October 2026, the gap becomes even more pronounced for Canadian teams budgeting in local currency.

ModelInput (USD/1M)Output (USD/1M)Input (approx. CAD/1M)Output (approx. CAD/1M)Cost for 10M output tokens (CAD)

GPT-6 Luna$0.10$0.50~$0.14~$0.69~$6.90

Claude Sonnet 5.5$2.00$10.00~$2.76~$13.80~$138.00

Grok 4.7 (≤200K prompt)$2.00$6.00~$2.76~$8.28~$82.80

Grok 4.7 (>200K prompt)$4.00$12.00~$5.52~$16.56~$165.60

Run the math on output tokens alone and GPT-6 Luna is roughly 20 times cheaper than Claude Sonnet 5.5 and 12 times cheaper than Grok 4.7’s short-prompt output rate. That is not a rounding error — for a support-ticket triage system processing millions of tokens a day, the difference between Luna and Sonnet 5.5 pricing is the difference between a four-figure and a five-figure monthly API bill. OpenAI’s own messaging around the Sol and Luna launch framed this directly: the company said it made caching and inference more efficient and passed the savings straight to developers, cutting API prices roughly 50 percent or more compared with the GPT-5.6 generation.

Claude Sonnet 5.5 did something different. Anthropic kept the per-token price identical to Sonnet 5 but improved throughput by more than 30 percent, meaning the effective cost per completed task drops even though the sticker price per token stayed flat. That is a meaningfully different pricing philosophy than OpenAI’s direct price cuts, and it matters for procurement teams comparing quotes: a static price list doesn’t tell you what Sonnet 5.5 will actually cost you to run a given workload versus its predecessor.

Grok 4.7’s tiered pricing is the most unusual of the three. Prompts under 200,000 tokens get the lower rate; cross that threshold and the entire request — not just the overage — gets billed at double the input rate and double the output rate. For teams doing long-document analysis or large codebase reviews, that cliff can double a bill overnight if requests aren’t chunked carefully.

Benchmark Performance: Intelligence, Coding, and Agentic Tasks

Raw capability is where this comparison gets more nuanced than price alone suggests. The Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index v4.3.2 — a composite benchmark built from ten separate evaluations including AA-Briefcase, GDPval-AA, AutomationBench-AA, Terminal-Bench 4.0, SciCode, and Humanity’s Last Exam — put Claude Sonnet 5.5 at 56 points as of October 3, 2026, landing it at #2 on the overall leaderboard behind only Claude Opus 5.5’s 58. That’s a remarkable result for a model explicitly marketed as the faster, lower-cost complement rather than the flagship.

Grok 4.7 scored closer to 46 on the same index according to a secondary Artificial Analysis report, putting it solidly mid-pack — ahead of budget-tier models but behind both Claude 5.5-generation models and GPT-6 Astra, which scored 53. GPT-6 Luna came in lowest among the three at 38.1 on the ModelGrep leaderboard’s October 2026 snapshot, which tracks speed and pricing alongside intelligence scoring.

On task-specific benchmarks, the picture shifts depending on what you’re measuring. On Terminal-Bench 4.0, a benchmark that stresses long-horizon command-line and agentic tasks, Grok 4.7 reportedly scored 37.6 percent on xAI’s own published chart, trailing both the GPT-6 and Claude families on that specific test. On CursorBench 4.0, a coding-focused benchmark, Grok 4.7 scored 51.8 percent by xAI’s own reporting — notably higher than GPT-6 Sol’s roughly 41.7 percent on the same test, suggesting Grok 4.7’s coding strengths show up more clearly in IDE-style agentic benchmarks than in pure terminal tasks.

GPT-6 Luna’s sibling data point is instructive here too. On the independent Vals AI Index, GPT-6 Luna ranked #20 of 65 models tested, scoring 58.45 percent at a cost of just $0.42 per test run — described by Vals AI as roughly 18 times cheaper than GPT-6 Sol’s 62.57 percent score at $7.56 per test. That is the clearest illustration of the entire budget-tier value proposition: Luna gives up roughly four percentage points of accuracy in exchange for an order-of-magnitude cost reduction.

It also helps to see these three alongside the flagship-tier siblings they sit underneath or beside, since none of them were built to be judged purely against each other in a vacuum. The table below lines up the benchmark figures gathered across Artificial Analysis, xAI’s own charts, and Anthropic’s Terminal-Bench 4.0 reporting.

ModelArtificial Analysis Intelligence IndexTerminal-Bench 4.0CursorBench 4.0 / codingNotes

GPT-6 Luna38.1Not published by OpenAINot a coding-focused tierBudget tier, high-volume tasks

Claude Sonnet 5.556 (#2 overall)Not separately broken out from Opus 5.5 reportingReported ~11 points above GPT-6 Sol by third-party analysisMid-tier flagship complement

Grok 4.7~4637.6%51.8%Coding and agentic focus, tiered pricing

GPT-6 Sol (reference)~52Not published by OpenAI~41.7%Luna’s pricier, coding-capable sibling

GPT-6 Astra (reference)5357.9%46.3% (xAI’s chart)OpenAI’s flagship model

Claude Opus 5.5 (reference)58 (#1 overall)66.4%~52.8% (xAI’s chart estimate)Anthropic’s flagship model

The pattern that emerges is consistent: every flagship model in this snapshot outscores its own cheaper sibling on raw intelligence, but the gap is far from uniform. Claude Sonnet 5.5 trails its own flagship Opus 5.5 by only two points on the Artificial Analysis Index, a remarkably tight margin for a model priced to be the budget-friendly option inside Anthropic’s own lineup. GPT-6 Luna, by contrast, trails its sibling GPT-6 Sol by roughly 14 points on the same type of index — a much wider capability gap in exchange for the much steeper price cut.

Speed and Latency: Which Model Responds Fastest

Throughput numbers matter just as much as intelligence scores for production systems with real-time user interaction. According to the ModelGrep leaderboard’s October 2026 snapshot, GPT-6 Luna generates tokens at roughly 149 tokens per second, making it the fastest of the three models measured. Grok 4.7, by comparison, registered around 90 tokens per second on the same leaderboard. Anthropic did not publish a raw tokens-per-second figure for Sonnet 5.5 in its own announcement, but the company’s stated claim — more than 30 percent faster than Sonnet 5 — implies throughput gains without a directly comparable absolute number against the other two models in this piece.

What that means practically: if your application is a chat widget, a voice assistant, or any interface where users notice a half-second delay, GPT-6 Luna’s raw speed advantage is real and measurable. If your application is an autonomous coding agent running for minutes or hours on a single task, raw tokens-per-second matters less than whether the model gets the task right the first time — which tilts the calculation back toward Sonnet 5.5 or Grok 4.7 depending on the specific task type.

Context Window and Multimodal Capability Compared

All three models now operate in the six-figure-to-million-token context range, which has quietly become table stakes for 2026-era frontier and near-frontier models. GPT-6 Luna and its sibling GPT-6 Sol both ship with a 1,050,000-token context window according to OpenAI’s developer documentation, with a shared 128,000-token maximum output ceiling. Claude Sonnet 5.5 sits close behind at a 1,000,000-token context window with the same 128,000-token output cap, per Anthropic’s own platform documentation.

Grok 4.7 is the outlier at 500,000 tokens — still enormous by pre-2026 standards, but half the ceiling of its two rivals here. xAI’s release notes confirm Grok 4.7 accepts text and image input but returns text-only output, with no stated cap on output length. Both GPT-6 Luna and Claude Sonnet 5.5 are documented as accepting text and image input as well, though detailed image-understanding benchmark results for Sonnet 5.5 specifically were not published in Anthropic’s public materials as of this writing.

For a practical frame of reference, a 500,000-token context window is still large enough to hold an entire mid-sized codebase or a few hundred pages of text in one pass. The million-token-plus windows on Luna and Sonnet 5.5 start to matter mainly for teams processing entire document archives, multi-hour meeting transcripts, or large multi-repo codebases in a single request without chunking.

Real-World Use Cases: Where Each Model Actually Fits

Benchmark scores only tell part of the story. Here’s how the three models map onto the kinds of workloads Canadian engineering and operations teams are actually running in late 2026.

High-volume customer support triage. A support queue processing thousands of tickets daily to classify intent, extract order numbers, and route to the right team is exactly the kind of “high-volume tasks with a clear goal” workload OpenAI built GPT-6 Luna for. At $0.50 per million output tokens, running this at scale is close to a rounding error on an operating budget.

Agentic coding assistants embedded in an IDE. Grok 4.7’s stronger showing on CursorBench 4.0 (51.8 percent by xAI’s own reporting) versus its weaker Terminal-Bench 4.0 result suggests it’s better suited to interactive, IDE-style coding assistance than fully autonomous command-line agents running unsupervised for long stretches.

Production code review and refactoring at mid-market scale. Claude Sonnet 5.5’s #2 ranking on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, combined with its 30-plus percent speed improvement over Sonnet 5, makes it a strong fit for teams that need near-flagship reasoning on code without paying Opus 5.5’s premium on every call.

Document summarization and extraction pipelines. GPT-6 Luna’s 1,050,000-token context window paired with its rock-bottom output pricing makes it a natural fit for ingesting long contracts, compliance documents, or research PDFs and returning structured extracts — provided the task doesn’t require deep multi-step reasoning.

Long-horizon autonomous agents handling professional work. Benchmarks like Agents’ Last Exam and AutomationBench, which test long-horizon tasks across dozens of sub-industries, are where flagship-adjacent models like Sonnet 5.5 and GPT-6 Sol (Luna’s pricier sibling) are reported to outperform budget-tier models by a wide margin — a sign that true multi-step agentic autonomy still rewards spending more per call.

Multimodal content moderation on image-heavy platforms. With both GPT-6 Luna and Grok 4.7 accepting image input, teams running moderation pipelines across large volumes of user-uploaded images have a genuine low-cost option in Luna, reserving a pricier model only for edge cases flagged as ambiguous.

Pros and Cons: GPT-6 Luna

Pros: Dramatically lower cost per token than either competitor in this comparison — roughly 20 times cheaper on output tokens than Claude Sonnet 5.5. Fastest raw throughput of the three at approximately 149 tokens per second. A full 1,050,000-token context window despite the budget pricing. Text and image input support at the same low price point.

Cons: Lowest Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index score of the three models compared here (38.1), meaning it will underperform on tasks requiring deep multi-step reasoning. Not designed or marketed for complex agentic or coding work — OpenAI itself frames it as a clerical and extraction tool, not a reasoning engine.

Pros and Cons: Claude Sonnet 5.5

Pros: Highest Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index score of the three (56, ranked #2 overall as of October 3, 2026). More than 30 percent faster than its predecessor Sonnet 5 at the same token price. Available across the Claude API, Amazon Bedrock, Claude Platform on AWS, Google Cloud, and Microsoft Foundry on day one, giving enterprise teams flexible deployment options. Strong fit for coding and reasoning-heavy work without flagship Opus 5.5 pricing.

Cons: By far the most expensive of the three on a per-token basis — 20 times GPT-6 Luna’s output price. Anthropic has not published a directly comparable tokens-per-second figure against GPT-6 Luna or Grok 4.7, making apples-to-apples latency comparisons harder for teams benchmarking providers.

Pros and Cons: Grok 4.7

Pros: Flexible four-tier reasoning effort system (low, medium, high, xhigh) lets developers dial cost and depth up or down per request. Strong CursorBench 4.0 coding score (51.8 percent by xAI’s own reporting) relative to some rivals. No published hard cap on output length. Mid-range pricing that undercuts Claude Sonnet 5.5 on short prompts.

Cons: Smallest context window of the three at 500,000 tokens. Tiered pricing structure means crossing the 200,000-token prompt threshold doubles the entire request’s rate, not just the overage — a costly surprise for teams that don’t actively chunk long inputs. Weaker Terminal-Bench 4.0 result (37.6 percent) suggests more limited strength on fully autonomous long-horizon command-line agent tasks.

Migration Guide: Switching Between These Three Models

If your team is currently running production workloads on an older-generation model and evaluating a move to one of these three, the practical migration path depends heavily on which direction you’re going.

Moving to GPT-6 Luna for cost savings

Start by auditing which of your current API calls are genuinely high-volume, low-complexity tasks — ticket classification, metadata extraction, short-form summarization. Run a side-by-side accuracy test on a sample of real production requests before fully cutting over, since Luna’s Artificial Analysis score sits meaningfully below flagship-tier models. Budget for a fallback path: route anything Luna flags as low-confidence or anything that fails a validation check to a stronger model like Sonnet 5.5 or GPT-6 Sol. This hybrid routing pattern is how most teams actually capture Luna’s cost advantage without quietly degrading product quality.

Moving to Claude Sonnet 5.5 from Sonnet 5 or Opus-tier models

Because Anthropic kept Sonnet 5.5’s per-token pricing identical to Sonnet 5, this is close to a drop-in upgrade for teams already on the Claude API, Bedrock, or Google Cloud’s Claude integration. Re-run your existing eval suite against Sonnet 5.5 before fully switching traffic over — Anthropic’s claimed speed and cost-efficiency improvements are workload-dependent, and the 30 percent figures are described as applying to most work, not universally. Teams currently paying Opus 5.5 pricing for tasks that don’t need frontier-level reasoning should specifically benchmark whether Sonnet 5.5 closes the capability gap enough to justify the cost reduction.

Moving to or from Grok 4.7

If you’re adopting Grok 4.7, the first engineering task is implementing prompt-length guardrails in your application layer to avoid accidentally crossing the 200,000-token pricing cliff. Chunk long documents proactively rather than letting requests grow organically. If you’re migrating away from Grok 4.7 toward GPT-6 Luna or Claude Sonnet 5.5, note that both target models accept a different context ceiling (1,050,000 and 1,000,000 tokens respectively versus Grok’s 500,000), so requests that were previously split across multiple Grok calls may be consolidatable into fewer calls on the new provider — worth re-architecting before go-live rather than after.

Which Model Should Canadian Businesses Choose in October 2026

There is no single winner here, and treating this as a horse race misses the point of why these three models exist in the first place. Each one was built to answer a different question about cost, speed, and capability.

If your workload is dominated by high-volume, low-complexity tasks — support ticket routing, metadata extraction, basic content moderation — GPT-6 Luna’s roughly 20-times cost advantage over Claude Sonnet 5.5 on output tokens is difficult to ignore, and its 149 tokens-per-second throughput keeps user-facing latency low. The trade-off is real: its Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index score of 38.1 means it will make more mistakes on anything resembling multi-step reasoning, so pair it with validation logic rather than trusting it blindly on ambiguous inputs.

If your workload involves production coding, technical reasoning, or any task where getting the answer right matters more than shaving pennies off the token bill, Claude Sonnet 5.5’s #2 position on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index — trailing only its own sibling Opus 5.5 — makes it the strongest all-around performer of the three, and its availability across AWS, Google Cloud, and Microsoft Foundry removes a lot of procurement friction for enterprise teams already standardized on one of those clouds.

If your workload is specifically agentic coding inside an IDE-style environment, Grok 4.7’s stronger CursorBench 4.0 result and flexible reasoning-effort dial make it worth evaluating directly against Sonnet 5.5 for that narrow use case — just build in prompt-length discipline to avoid its pricing cliff.

The broader signal from this three-model snapshot is that the AI market has stopped converging on one best model and started fragmenting into task-specific tiers. That is good news for budget-conscious Canadian teams, provided they’re willing to do the benchmarking work rather than defaulting to whichever provider’s marketing lands loudest.

How These Models Fit Into the Broader September 2026 AI Release Wave

GPT-6 Luna, Claude Sonnet 5.5, and Grok 4.7 did not launch in isolation. They were three releases among more than a dozen that shipped across the AI industry in September 2026 alone, spanning Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, DeepSeek, Meta, Alibaba’s Qwen team, and xAI. Tracking sites that monitor release cadence counted at least 15 major model releases in September 2026 under a narrow definition, and as many as 32 under a broader counting method that includes minor variants and regional releases.

That pace matters for procurement planning. A model that looks like the best option in early October could be superseded within weeks, as OpenAI, Anthropic, and xAI have all demonstrated a pattern of rapid iterative releases rather than infrequent, big-bang launches. Claude Sonnet 5.5 itself is explicitly described by Anthropic as the second model in the Claude 5.5 family — with a corresponding Haiku 5.5 release expected to round out the lineup, according to Anthropic’s platform documentation. Teams building long-term infrastructure around any single model’s API should plan for version churn as the default state of this market, not an exception.

OpenAI’s own framing of the Sol and Luna launch, detailed in Unite.AI’s coverage of the announcement, underscores how deliberate this tiering strategy has become. Rather than releasing a single do-everything model, OpenAI now ships three distinct price-to-capability points under one generation name, and expects developers to pick the right one per task rather than defaulting to the flagship for everything. Anthropic’s parallel move with Sonnet 5.5, reported in detail by 9to5Mac’s breakdown of the release, follows the same logic: replace the previous mid-tier model with one that is faster and cheaper to run per completed task, without touching the flagship Opus tier at all.

Why This Three-Way Split Reflects a Bigger Shift in the AI Market

Until relatively recently, the AI model market worked roughly like a single-ladder competition: one lab’s flagship against another’s, with the losing model simply discounted until the next release cycle. What GPT-6 Luna, Claude Sonnet 5.5, and Grok 4.7 show instead is a market that has split horizontally as well as vertically. Each lab is now running at least two or three simultaneous product lines — a flagship for maximum capability, a mid-tier for cost-conscious production work, and in OpenAI’s case, a third tier purpose-built for high-volume clerical automation.

This matters for how Canadian businesses should think about vendor selection. Comparing “OpenAI vs Anthropic vs xAI” as if each company offers one product is no longer a useful framing. The real comparison is tier-to-tier: GPT-6 Luna against other high-volume budget models, Claude Sonnet 5.5 against other mid-tier reasoning models, and Grok 4.7 against other coding-and-agentic specialists. A team evaluating providers without that distinction risks comparing a $0.50-per-million-token model against a $10-per-million-token model and drawing the wrong conclusion about which “company” offers better value — when the real answer depends entirely on which tier within each company’s lineup actually matches the workload.

The tiering strategy also changes how fast a team can respond to cost pressure. Because GPT-6 Luna, Claude Sonnet 5.5, and comparable mid-tier models now share largely compatible API shapes with their flagship siblings, switching a specific workload down a tier — or up one, if accuracy complaints start showing up — has become closer to a configuration change than a full re-architecture. That flexibility is arguably a bigger deal for most production teams than any single benchmark score in this comparison.

Integration Code Example: Switching Providers With Minimal Rework

Because all three providers expose OpenAI-compatible or near-compatible chat completion endpoints, teams building provider-agnostic routing layers can abstract model selection behind a thin wrapper. Here’s a simplified pattern for routing requests to the cheapest viable model first, falling back to a stronger model when needed.

def route_request(prompt, complexity_score):

if complexity_score < 0.3:

# High-volume, low-complexity: GPT-6 Luna

return call_model("gpt-6-luna", prompt, max_tokens=2000)

elif complexity_score < 0.7:

# Mid-complexity coding or reasoning: Claude Sonnet 5.5

return call_model("claude-sonnet-5-5", prompt, max_tokens=4000)

else:

# Agentic/coding with long context needs: Grok 4.7

# Chunk prompt if approaching the 200K token pricing threshold

if estimate_tokens(prompt) > 190000:

prompt = chunk_prompt(prompt, max_tokens=190000)

return call_model("grok-4.7", prompt, reasoning_effort="high")

This kind of complexity-based routing is becoming standard practice for teams trying to control API spend without sacrificing output quality on the tasks that actually need a stronger model. The key engineering investment isn’t the routing logic itself — it’s building a reliable complexity scorer that correctly predicts which tier a given request actually needs.

Data Residency and Enterprise Considerations for Canadian Teams

None of the three companies in this comparison currently operates a dedicated Canadian data residency region for these specific models, based on their public documentation as of October 2026. Claude Sonnet 5.5’s availability through Amazon Bedrock, Google Cloud, and Microsoft Foundry gives Canadian enterprise customers an indirect path to regional data handling options through those cloud providers’ existing Canadian infrastructure, which is a meaningful procurement advantage for regulated industries like finance and healthcare that need to document where data is processed. OpenAI’s GPT-6 Luna and xAI’s Grok 4.7 are both currently accessed primarily through each company’s direct API, without the same multi-cloud distribution pattern Anthropic has built out for Sonnet 5.5.

For Canadian businesses in regulated sectors, this difference in distribution strategy is worth weighing alongside raw price and benchmark performance — the cheapest model on a per-token basis isn’t necessarily the easiest one to get approved through a compliance review.

Common Mistakes Teams Make Choosing Between These Three

After watching how quickly teams jump on new model releases, a handful of avoidable mistakes keep showing up in how companies evaluate GPT-6 Luna, Claude Sonnet 5.5, and Grok 4.7 against each other.

Benchmarking on synthetic prompts instead of real production traffic. Public benchmark scores like the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index are useful for ranking models against each other in general, but they rarely match the exact distribution of prompts a specific application sends. A model that scores lower on a generic index can still outperform a higher-scoring rival on your specific task if that task happens to play to its strengths.

Ignoring the Grok 4.7 pricing cliff until the first invoice arrives. Because the 200,000-token threshold reprices the entire request rather than just the overage, teams that don’t actively monitor prompt length can see costs double without any code change on their end — simply because user-submitted content grew past the threshold on a subset of requests.

Assuming GPT-6 Luna’s price cut means a proportional capability cut. The jump from GPT-6 Sol’s Artificial Analysis score to GPT-6 Luna’s is roughly 14 points, while the price difference between the two is closer to 20 times on a per-token basis. The two numbers don’t move in lockstep, and teams that assume they do either overpay for Sol when Luna would do the job, or underestimate how much accuracy they’re giving up by defaulting to Luna everywhere.

Treating “faster” and “cheaper” as the same claim for Claude Sonnet 5.5. Anthropic’s 30 percent improvement claims cover speed and effective cost together, but they are not identical metrics, and the company has been explicit that the improvement applies to “most work” rather than universally. Workloads with unusual prompt shapes should be benchmarked directly rather than assumed to inherit the published average.

Skipping a fallback path entirely when adopting a budget-tier model. The teams getting the most value out of GPT-6 Luna are generally the ones that pair it with a confidence check and a fallback route to a stronger model, not the ones that route 100 percent of a workload to the cheapest option and hope the accuracy numbers hold up in production the same way they did in testing.

Rate Limits, Availability, and Developer Experience

Beyond raw pricing and benchmark scores, the day-to-day developer experience differs meaningfully across these three APIs. GPT-6 Luna and GPT-6 Sol are both accessible through OpenAI’s standard API, through Codex, and through select ChatGPT plans — OpenAI has stated that free and Go-tier ChatGPT users can also try Luna directly in the desktop application, which is a notably lower barrier to entry than either of its two rivals here offers for casual testing.

Claude Sonnet 5.5’s multi-cloud distribution is the standout feature of its developer experience. Being available simultaneously through the direct Claude API, Amazon Bedrock, the Claude Platform on AWS, Google Cloud, and Microsoft Foundry means a team already running infrastructure on any of those three major clouds can adopt Sonnet 5.5 without introducing a new billing relationship or a new network egress path — a genuinely practical advantage for larger organizations with established cloud procurement processes.

Grok 4.7’s developer experience centers on its own API with reasoning-effort controls exposed directly as a request parameter, giving developers fine-grained control that neither of the other two models exposes in quite the same explicit way. The trade-off is a narrower distribution footprint — as of this writing, Grok 4.7 is primarily a direct-API product rather than one distributed across third-party cloud marketplaces the way Claude Sonnet 5.5 is.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is GPT-6 Luna cheaper than Claude Sonnet 5.5?

Yes, significantly. GPT-6 Luna is priced at $0.10 per million input tokens and $0.50 per million output tokens, compared to Claude Sonnet 5.5’s $2.00 input and $10.00 output per million tokens. That makes Luna roughly 20 times cheaper on output tokens, according to each company’s published API pricing.

Which model has the largest context window?

GPT-6 Luna has the largest context window of the three at 1,050,000 tokens, just ahead of Claude Sonnet 5.5’s 1,000,000 tokens. Grok 4.7 has the smallest at 500,000 tokens, according to each provider’s developer documentation.

Which of these three models scores highest on benchmarks?

Claude Sonnet 5.5 scores highest on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index v4.3.2, reaching 56 points and ranking #2 overall as of October 3, 2026, behind only its sibling Claude Opus 5.5. Grok 4.7 scored approximately 46, and GPT-6 Luna scored 38.1 on the same type of composite intelligence benchmark, per ModelGrep’s October 2026 leaderboard.

Is Grok 4.7 good for coding tasks?

Grok 4.7 shows mixed results depending on the specific coding benchmark. It scored 51.8 percent on CursorBench 4.0, an IDE-style coding benchmark, according to xAI’s own published chart — a relatively strong result. On Terminal-Bench 4.0, which tests long-horizon command-line agent tasks, it scored lower at 37.6 percent by the same source, suggesting it performs better in interactive coding assistance than in fully autonomous long-running agent tasks.

Does Claude Sonnet 5.5 cost more than Sonnet 5?

No. Anthropic kept Claude Sonnet 5.5’s per-token pricing identical to Sonnet 5 at $2.00 input and $10.00 output per million tokens, while stating the new model runs more than 30 percent faster and costs up to 30 percent less for most work in practical, effective terms due to the speed improvement.

What happens if a Grok 4.7 prompt goes over 200,000 tokens?

According to xAI’s developer release notes, once a prompt exceeds 200,000 tokens, the entire request is billed at the higher tier: $4.00 per million input tokens and $12.00 per million output tokens, versus $2.00 and $6.00 respectively for prompts under that threshold. This applies to the full request, not just the portion above 200,000 tokens, which makes prompt-length management an important cost-control step.

Can I use GPT-6 Luna for coding tasks?

GPT-6 Luna is not positioned by OpenAI as a coding-focused model. The company describes it as suited for high-volume tasks with a clear goal, like summarizing documents, extracting information, or answering quick questions, while its sibling GPT-6 Sol is the model OpenAI designed specifically for more complex tasks including coding. Teams needing budget-tier coding assistance should evaluate GPT-6 Sol or benchmark Luna carefully against their specific codebase before relying on it for production code generation.

Are these three models available through cloud providers like AWS or Google Cloud?

Claude Sonnet 5.5 is available through the Claude API, Amazon Bedrock, Claude Platform on AWS, Google Cloud, and Microsoft Foundry, according to Anthropic’s own release notes. GPT-6 Luna is accessed primarily through OpenAI’s own API, Codex, and select ChatGPT plans. Grok 4.7 is available through the xAI API directly, based on current public documentation from each company.

articles.headline: ChatGPT, Gemini and Google never name 9 of 40 UK software firms in shortlists - PPC Land
articles.body: ChatGPT, Gemini and Google never name 9 of 40 UK software firms in shortlists    PPC Land

scored.body:
Nine of 40 UK B2B software companies were named in none of the 24 shortlist answers they received from four AI platforms, according to The AI Shortlist 2026, a report Recrawled published on September 29, 2026. The same research reports YouTube in 25% of Google AI Overview answers about the companies and in none of the 360 ChatGPT answers.In ShortA UK agency put 1,608 questions of the kind software buyers type to ChatGPT, Gemini and two Google search tools, then checked which British software companies came back in the answers. Nine of the 40 companies it studied closely were never recommended on any of the four tools when a buyer asked who to consider, even though every one of the 40 was recognised once its name was typed in. So a company's place in an AI answer depends on how the question is worded and which tool is asked, and the results describe one day, September 4, 2026, rather than a permanent ranking.A one-day snapshot of 1,608 questionsRecrawled describes itself as an answer engine optimisation (AEO) agency, and The AI Shortlist 2026 was researched by two of its co-founders, Jess Brookes and Charles Törnros. The study began with 200 UK-headquartered B2B software companies, each with between 20 and 150 staff and selling a specialist product to other organisations. They were spread across seven sectors: contact centre and customer experience, HR and workforce, compliance and risk, fintech and insurtech, supply chain and field service, healthtech and edtech, and other specialist software. According to the report, each company was checked against its own website, its filings and its review-site listings rather than pulled from a list. Forty were then studied in depth, in 33 buyer categories across six of the seven sectors.The questions went to ChatGPT, Gemini, Google AI Overviews and Google AI Mode, each in default mode, signed out and with the location set to the UK. The run took place on September 4, 2026. In all, 1,608 questions were put: 168 to the sectors (six broad questions per sector, on each of four platforms) and 1,440 about the 40 companies. Every studied company received nine questions, six asking which companies to shortlist and three asking about the company by name. On four platforms that comes to 36 answers per company, 24 to the shortlist questions and 12 to the by-name ones. Of the 1,608 questions, 1,600 produced answers. The remaining eight were by-name questions for which Google displayed no AI Overview, and the report records that outcome as a result in its own right.The six shortlist questions covered different buying situations. Three say UK or name a UK buyer. One drops the country and names the size of the buyer instead, one starts from the market leader's name, and one is a head-to-head between the leader and its nearest rival. In the report's example, the UK-specific wording asks about court bundling software for a UK law firm, while the size-based version asks about court bundling software for mid-sized law firms.Recognised, but not recommendedThe executive summary carries its argument in a heading: "Being recognised by AI is not the same as making the shortlist." When checked by name, all 40 companies were correctly identified by at least one platform, according to Recrawled. Asking which companies to consider produced a different picture. Twenty-nine were named on at least one shortlist question that specified the UK, two were named only when the question did not say UK, and nine were named in none of their 24 shortlist answers, on any platform. No company appeared in all 24. The most any managed was 22.Wording changed the resultFour of the six shortlist questions tested the same companies in different buying situations. A company counts in the report's chart if any of the four platforms named it anywhere in the answer; the final column is the appendix's count of individual answers.

Question typeCompanies named by at least one platformIndividual answers naming the companyUK-specific shortlist question63% (25 of 40)36% (173 of 480)Mid-sized buyer, no "UK"43% (17 of 40)22% (35 of 160)Alternatives to the market leader13% (5 of 39)4% (6 of 156)Market leader against nearest rival0% (0 of 38)0% (0 of 152)

One company was excluded from the alternatives question and two from the head-to-head question because their own product was the subject. For the same reason the answer-level figures add up to 948 rather than 960: 12 answers in which a company's own product was the subject are left out. The company was named in 11 of those 12, so across all 960 answers it was named 225 times, or 23%.The first two question types were equally specific, according to the report, so the drop was not simply the result of narrower wording. In one category, removing "UK" was enough for three of the four platforms to switch to companies based outside the UK. A buyer asking for alternatives to the market leader is "explicitly looking beyond the market leader", yet only 13% of the companies studied appeared in those answers. The fourth question set the market leader versus its nearest rival. None of the other 38 companies showed up in any of the four platform answers, according to Recrawled; AI sometimes introduced another brand, just never one of the companies studied. Because that prompt already names two vendors, the result measures whether a third name found room in the answer, which is narrower than general invisibility.The platforms disagreedOf the 31 companies named on at least one platform, Gemini never named 13 (42%), Google AI Mode 11 (35%), Google AI Overviews six (19%) and ChatGPT five (16%). Across the same 240 shortlist questions, Google AI Overviews named the studied companies 69 times and AI Mode 44. Google's two AI experiences therefore differed substantially from each other, according to the report.Other datasets point toward platform divergence as well. The Semrush AI Visibility Index, covered by PPC Land on June 30, 2026, analysed 126 million US prompts from January to April 2026 and found that only 36 of more than 1,200 brands kept top-100 status on every platform in every month studied. In that index the mention-source overlap, which Semrush reports by platform, was 64% on AI Overviews and 30% on Gemini, and the average number of brands named per response ran from 3.3 on ChatGPT to 5.2 on AI Mode.Video citations separate Google from the other platformsAccording to the report, YouTube appeared in 25% of Google AI Overview answers and 19% of AI Mode answers about the 40 companies. For Gemini the share was 2%, and ChatGPT showed none in its 360 answers. The wording shifts within the document, though: pages 5 and 10 say YouTube "appeared", while the appendix says the answers "cited at least one video". Counted by citations rather than answers, YouTube was 3.3% of the 7,704 citations across every answer the researchers read, and by distinct pages it was 4% of 2,750 pages on 1,223 websites.Measurements elsewhere differ by platform, market and method. Meltwater's analysis for August 2026, reported by PPC Land on September 23, tracked eight systems including ChatGPT and ranked YouTube the most-cited platform across all eight. Recrawled's zero for ChatGPT sits apart from that finding. The datasets differ in query type, market, period and measure, and the report does not address Meltwater's work. Tinuiti's Q2 2026 report, in the same article, found that YouTube citations in AI Mode more than quadrupled between January and April 2026, and in AI Overviews more than doubled.Cited, but not recommendedEight of the 40 companies had their own pages cited in answers that recommended somebody else, across 19 answers, according to the report. One vendor selling software that checks suppliers' security had published a guide to the best software in its category. AI cited the guide in nine shortlist answers. In four of them, it used the vendor's content but recommended other companies. In the report's usage, cited means the answer displayed the page as one of its sources, while named means the company itself appeared in the answer.The report's source breakdown shows where the cited material came from. Of the 2,750 distinct pages, 67% were on software vendors' own websites, 9% on review directories, 4% on YouTube, 3% on official and industry bodies, 3% on press, blogs and forums, and 14% on other sites. Pages were classified by website, with vendor sites matched against every brand named in the run and a random 100 read by hand as a check. Around a quarter of the pages cited in each company's shortlist answers sat on the websites of the most frequently named companies in its category.A separate study points at a similar gap between being cited and being chosen. Scrunch, which sells AI visibility monitoring, analysed roughly 10,000 AI-cited URLs and found that when a brand's own ranked list was cited, the brand's recommendation rate rose from about 4% to roughly 7%, and its mention rate from about 19% to 39%. A competitor was recommended instead of the author 24.3% of the time. PPC Land reported the study, which covered data collected from May 17 to June 30, 2026, in late September.Review counts did not track namingAcross the 40 companies, the correlation between review volume and AI naming was -0.06, which the report calls effectively zero. The company named most often had 19 Capterra reviews and no G2 listing, and it appeared in 22 of its 24 answers. One company with 637 reviews was named in just one of 24. Among the ten companies named most, the typical company had two to three reviews across G2 and Capterra; among the nine never named, the typical company had 13. Counts were taken from G2 and Capterra on the day of the run, and a missing listing counted as zero.The report is careful about what this does and does not show. Finding no link, it says, is "not proof there is no link anywhere". Among the companies named most, Recrawled says it repeatedly saw specific third-party proof and measurable facts in the answers and pages that named them, which it describes as "an observed pattern, not evidence that those signals caused the naming".Buyer behaviour gives some context. A Semrush survey of 519 B2B buyers who use AI tools for work, published by PPC Land on July 20, 2026, found that 92% said AI had shaped their vendor shortlist and 66% had spotted vendors missing from AI answers. Only 7% said brand recognition determines whether they notice a vendor in AI responses, against 53% who prioritise a close match with their specific use case. And 38% checked reviews on G2 or similar sites after receiving an AI recommendation.Dominant brands, and room beneath themOf the 33 buyer categories, 61% had one dominant brand appearing in at least three-quarters of the answers. Even so, 50% of the 40 companies took first position on at least one buyer question. Each category received the same six shortlist questions on four platforms, so 24 answers, read once for each company in it.The limit of a strong position shows in one example. A vendor that was not the leader in its category was named in 16 of its 24 answers, on all four platforms, in much the same terms each time. When the buyer asked for alternatives to the leader, or compared the leader with its nearest rival, it was named in none of those eight answers.The appendix adds a wider view. On the six broad sector questions, separate from the shortlist set, 23 of the 200 companies were named at all, and global brands dominated. Contact centre and customer experience software returned 54 different brand names, one of them in 17 of that sector's 24 answers; fintech and insurtech returned 98.Accuracy once the buyer knows the nameThe sixth finding moves from visibility to correctness. Of the 40 companies checked by name on four platforms, one in three got at least one answer about the wrong business, two in five had review questions answered using employee-review sites, and one in five had pricing come back inconsistently or without a source. Thirteen of the 40 shared a name with an unrelated business or product.The report lists four examples:A UK desk-booking vendor was answered as a restaurant and cocktail bar in Northampton, by ChatGPT.A UK contact-centre vendor was answered as a Continental car tyre, by Gemini and Google AI Overviews.A UK insurance-data vendor was answered as a Dyson robot vacuum cleaner, by Gemini and Google AI Mode.A UK cyber-risk vendor was answered as a cannabis producer, by Gemini.The employee-review problem has a quotable case. Google AI Mode reproduced an employee-review site verbatim in response to a reviews question for one vendor: "Was a great company, on the decline." Elsewhere in its answers, according to the report, AI Mode had called that vendor's product "the gold standard".Same-name confusion has appeared outside B2B software. In July 2026, a Google AI Overview told searchers that Anna Mae's Bakery and Restaurant in Millbank, Ontario was closing on July 31; the closure belonged to a different business of the same name in Illinois.Why the findings matter to marketing teamsThe report opens with three figures from other organisations. According to 6sense's 2025 B2B Buyer Experience Report, covering nearly 4,000 buyers, 95% of purchases went to a vendor already on the buyer's Day One shortlist. Forrester's 2026 report The State Of Business Buying, with nearly 18,000 buyers, found that 94% of business buyers used AI while buying. TrustRadius, in its 2026 B2B Buying Disconnect Report of 1,862 buyers, found that 83% of technology buyers shortlisted three or fewer products, with an average shortlist of 2.7. Recrawled's framing is that the list is short, forms early, and now passes in part through AI.Other numbers point the same way. Bain data cited in a LinkedIn marketing blog post, and covered by PPC Land on May 26, 2026, put the share of B2B buyers who start with a day-one vendor list at 86%, with 81% buying from it. Whether marketing teams can see their position on that list is a separate question. An index from Agentcy found that 81% of 104 senior B2B marketing leaders consider AI visibility a blind spot and that only 10% can consistently connect AI-driven touchpoints to revenue. PPC Land reported it on March 5, 2026.Software vendors have started to build measurement for the gap. HubSpot's AEO tool, reported on April 14, 2026, tracks brand visibility in ChatGPT, Gemini and Perplexity and costs $50 a month as a standalone product. Cloudflare opened an AEO Visibility Dashboard in early access on August 6, 2026, covering Claude and GPT models. Recrawled's study differs in form: one fixed day, a defined sample, and separate counts per question type and per platform, which the report argues a single blended score would hide.Recrawled's recommendations and commercial positionEach finding in the report ends with a recommendation box. Recrawled recommends building visibility around the buying situations that matter rather than one broad category question, and tracking platforms separately instead of as a blended score. It also recommends content that shows why a company belongs on the shortlist for the problems it solves, specific proof rather than review volume as the goal, consistent category, pricing and product claims across sources, and a focus on the situations where a company has the strongest reason to win.The authors also sell services in this area. According to the report, Recrawled offers diagnosis and setup, repair and optimisation, and management and continuity, plus a free AI Shortlist Assessment covering ChatGPT, Gemini, Google AI Overviews, Google AI Mode and Claude, delivered by email within three working days. The companies studied were not contacted and took no part in the research, according to the report.What the data does not showThe report states its limits. It is "a snapshot of one day", and 40 companies are "a sample, not a census". Recrawled notes that the same questions asked the next day may produce different answers on all four platforms, and that nothing in the study predicts what any platform will say next. SISTRIX's 17-week measurement across three platforms and six countries gives a sense of the movement involved: AI Mode rotated 56% of its citations each week and ChatGPT 74%, while AI Overviews stayed completely stable for just over half of queries, according to the analysis PPC Land reported on April 30, 2026.Recrawled also separates citation from cause. The platforms report which pages they cited, not why they named the companies they named, so a cited page is an observation and not an explanation of a recommendation.Two presentation points stand out in the document itself. The executive summary counts 29 companies named on at least one UK-specific shortlist question, while the first bar in the wording chart shows 25 for the UK-specific question type, and the report does not set out the four-company difference in so many words. The YouTube figure is described as appearance in one place and as citing at least one video in another. Neither changes the headline count of nine companies named in none of their 24 shortlist answers, but both leave open exactly which answers each percentage covers. Fuller methodology is available from Recrawled on request, according to the report.TimelineMarch 5, 2026 - Agentcy index finds 81% of 104 senior B2B marketing leaders call AI visibility a blind spot.April 14, 2026 - HubSpot adds a standalone AEO tool tracking ChatGPT, Gemini and Perplexity.April 30, 2026 - SISTRIX 17-week analysis is reported, showing AI Mode rotating 56% of citations weekly and ChatGPT 74%.May 26, 2026 - Bain figures on day-one vendor lists are reported: 86% of B2B buyers start with one, 81% buy from it.June 30, 2026 - Semrush AI Visibility Index shows 36 of more than 1,200 brands holding top-100 status on every platform.July 18-19, 2026 - An AI Overview wrongly says an Ontario bakery is closing on July 31.July 20, 2026 - Semrush B2B buyer survey results are published: 92% say AI shaped their vendor shortlist.August 6, 2026 - Cloudflare opens its AEO Visibility Dashboard in early access.September 4, 2026 - Recrawled puts 1,608 questions to ChatGPT, Gemini, Google AI Overviews and Google AI Mode.September 23, 2026 - Meltwater and Tinuiti YouTube citation data is reported.September 24, 2026 - Scrunch study on self-ranked lists and AI recommendations is reported.September 29, 2026 - Recrawled publishes The AI Shortlist 2026.Semrush: 36 brands win AI visibility everywhere, 1,200 vanish on one - Semrush's index of 126 million US prompts compares brand visibility across AI platforms from January to April 2026.Brand recognition sways just 7% of B2B AI buyers, Semrush finds - a survey of 519 B2B buyers on how AI shapes vendor shortlists and what they check afterwards.Self-ranked brands gain AI recommendations from 4% to 7%, Scrunch finds - an analysis of roughly 10,000 AI-cited URLs on what happens when a brand's own list is cited.Google switched on AI Mode checkout for Shopify stores without asking - an article that also carries Meltwater and Tinuiti data on YouTube citations across AI systems.SISTRIX April 2026: AI citation drift and the death of keyword research - a 17-week measurement of how much AI citations change from week to week.Google AI Overview forces Anna Mae's Bakery to deny fake July 31 closing - a case of an AI Overview confusing two same-name businesses.LinkedIn's three-phase B2B launch framework: why one day is not enough - includes Bain figures on day-one vendor lists and purchases.Most B2B marketers can't prove AI's role in their pipeline - Agentcy's index of 104 senior B2B marketing leaders on AI visibility and revenue attribution.HubSpot launches AEO tool as organic traffic drops 27% for its customers - details of HubSpot's AI visibility tracker and its pricing.Cloudflare scores brand visibility inside Claude and GPT answers - Cloudflare's early-access dashboard for citation rate, mention rate and share of voice.SummaryWho: Recrawled, a UK answer engine optimisation agency, through its co-founders Jess Brookes and Charles Törnros. The subjects were 200 UK-headquartered B2B software companies with 20 to 150 staff, of which 40 were studied in depth. The platforms queried were ChatGPT, Gemini, Google AI Overviews and Google AI Mode.What: A report titled The AI Shortlist 2026, based on 1,608 questions and 1,600 answers. Nine of the 40 companies were named in none of their 24 shortlist answers. Named share fell from 63% to 43% to 13% to 0% as the question moved from a UK-specific shortlist to a no-country version, to alternatives to the leader, to a leader-versus-rival comparison. YouTube appeared in 25% of AI Overview answers and none of ChatGPT's 360, and review volume showed a correlation of -0.06 with naming.When: The research was run on September 4, 2026 and published on September 29, 2026.Where: The questions were asked with each platform in default mode, signed out and with the location set to the UK, about UK B2B software companies.Why: Recrawled set out to learn what gets a B2B software company into an AI shortlist, citing figures that buyers form short lists early and increasingly use AI. The report's authors sell AEO services, and the study is a one-day sample of 40 companies, which Recrawled itself describes as not a census.

articles.body: Google unveils Gemini 4 Argon, its new frontier model    Yahoo Tech

scored.body: Google announced its new frontier model, Gemini 4 Argon, which is initially rolling out to trusted cyber defenders through its Fairwind Program, a limited-access initiative by Google DeepMind and Google Cloud.The company said Argon is designed for complex, long-running tasks across software engineering, legal and financial work, and cybersecurity. It will initially be available to paid API customers and Google AI Ultra subscribers.Argon will launch at a $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens, with cached input tokens priced at a 95% discount. Google has also increased the model's output limit to 1 million tokens from 64,000 tokens.Google said Argon is already being used internally for coding, research and writing. The model helped quantum computing researchers beat a published optimization baseline by 40% in one case and identified memory improvements that could save up to 1 PiB across Google's data centers.Argon agents are also helping migrate C/C++ code to Rust. For Google's libgav1 video decoder, the agents replaced 32,000 lines of SIMD code, producing a Rust version that Google said runs 2.7 times faster than the previous Rust version.Google is also strengthening safeguards against misuse, prompt injection and model misalignment before broader availability.

members.title: RFK Jr. Wants to AI-ify Health Care. Claude Says He’s Full of Sh*t. - The Bulwark

representative.headline: RFK Jr. Wants to AI-ify Health Care. Claude Says He’s Full of Sh*t. - The Bulwark
representative.body: RFK Jr. Wants to AI-ify Health Care. Claude Says He’s Full of Sh*t.    The Bulwark

articles.headline: RFK Jr. Wants to AI-ify Health Care. Claude Says He’s Full of Sh*t. - The Bulwark
articles.body: RFK Jr. Wants to AI-ify Health Care. Claude Says He’s Full of Sh*t.    The Bulwark

scored.body: (Photo illustration by Bill Kuchman/The Bulwark | Photos: Getty, Shutterstock, Claude)ROBERT F. KENNEDY JR. BECOMING a huge AI cheerleader probably wasn’t on your 2026 bingo card. It certainly wasn’t on mine.But there was Kennedy on Tuesday, speaking in his capacity as the secretary of health and human services, talking about the potential of artificial intelligence to help pinpoint what’s wrong with people when they are sick or injured.“It would be malpractice for a doctor to make a diagnosis, or to make a prescription, without at least checking AI,” Kennedy said at a MAHA Action conference in Washington.1MAHA, of course, stands for “Make America Healthy Again,” the movement that Kennedy has been leading, which is known for its hostility to all things artificial. But Kennedy doesn’t see AI as yet another way for science to disrupt the natural order. Rather, he said to the MAHA attendees, AI will let average people challenge the establishment of doctors and scientists, and make up their own minds about what constitutes good medical care.As an example, Kennedy suggested how people could have used AI during the COVID pandemic, when public health officials promoted vaccination as a way to protect the elderly and others with weaker immune systems. “If somebody tells you that a vaccine will prevent transmission and infection, or you need to take it to protect your grandmother, AI may say it actually doesn’t do that,” Kennedy said.Or to put it more bluntly, as Kennedy did later, AI would “free us from medical tyranny.”It might surprise you to hear I think Kennedy is right about the potential of AI to transform medicine, and in a good way. Some of the most promising possible uses of AI—assuming it doesn’t, you know, extinguish humanity—lie in its ability to help providers make more accurate diagnoses.The immense value of AI systems in making diagnoses in fields where they can be trained on enormous datasets has been widely recognized over the past few years; for example, in diagnostic imaging, by training on vast numbers of x-rays, CT scans, MRIs, and ultrasounds, AI systems can detect diagnostic patterns too subtle or complex for even experienced clinicians to detect consistently.The potential value of AI is also growing in fields like cancer treatment, where the sheer volume of relevant clinical information is so great—and changing so quickly—that even the most capable oncologists can’t keep it all in their heads.“The data are pretty good that AI is more accurate than physicians at creating a differential diagnosis,” Ezekiel Emanuel, the University of Pennsylvania oncologist, bioethicist, and author, told me over email. He and two collaborators recently generated some controversy by suggesting in a Journal of the American Medical Association article that medical decision-making by AI alone was frequently superior to decision-making by doctors who merely consult AI. But, Emanuel told me, you don’t even have to believe that to see the upside potential.“In many cases there is not going to be a need to check with AI,” Emanuel said. “But in hard cases, there may be good reason to check with AI. All physicians have had ‘tough cases’ that do not exactly fit with symptoms or lab tests that puzzle them.”AI could also boost health care by operating as a force multiplier: It can enable professionals without the full training of a doctor to provide front-line medical care in places where doctors are in short supply.Experts have talked for years about tapping that potential as a way to help some of the most impoverished parts of the world—or even impoverished parts of the United States. And in the past few months, Mehmet Oz, administrator of the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services, has been touting AI’s potential as a way to address provider shortages in rural areas.The reason AI can do all of that is that it excels at gathering, digesting, and applying information—including scientific data. And this characteristic makes it useful for debunking charlatans, cranks, and conspiracy theorists, including those peddling unfounded claims about the dangers of vaccines.In other words, it’s a terrific fact-checker for Kennedy, as I discovered myself last week.INSPIRED BY HIS CALL TO USE AI, I went ahead and asked Claude (Anthropic’s AI assistant) to analyze some of Kennedy’s more memorable statements. I used the professional, paid version, because it provides access to more capable AI models that can produce more accurate results, and I started with one of Kennedy’s favorite claims: that the scientific community hasn’t seriously investigated links between vaccines and autism.Kennedy has cited this alleged failing to justify his agenda of unwinding federal support for vaccines. A version of the statement now even appears on the website of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. To get an accurate read on it, I fed Claude a recent version of Kennedy’s linkage between vaccines and autism—one he gave just a few weeks ago during a speech to Children’s Health Defense, the organization that he led from 2015 to 2023 and that has done as much as any to undermine faith in vaccines.Here was the quote, which refers to eighteen vaccines the CDC has been recommending for children:In fact, of all of those ninety-four doses of the eighteen vaccines, only one of them was subject to a placebo control trial and that was the COVID vaccine. The other ones were like this. There was no safety study. We have no idea what the risk profile is for these products. And you know that means we can’t really make the kind of risk-benefit analysis that my agency is supposed to do.Claude’s verdict:The first misleading claim was on the number of doses (which Kennedy inflated). The second was about the supposed lack of placebo testing, which Kennedy says all the time and which—as infectious-disease experts like Stanford University’s Jake Scott have noted repeatedly—is simply not true. As for the third claim, that “there was no safety study,” here’s Claude’s take:This is the most clearly false part, and it goes further than the placebo claim. A trial without a placebo is still a safety study. Head-to-head trials against existing vaccines collect safety data, and so does post-licensure surveillance. . . . The HHS website itself says every authorized or approved vaccine goes through safety testing, including clinical trials and monitoring after reaching the market. The 2013 [Institute of Medicine] report on the schedule, which Kennedy cited in this same speech, found no evidence that the schedule is unsafe.The kernel of truth in Kennedy’s argument (which Claude duly noted) is that scientists don’t typically test new versions of old vaccines against placebos. They test new vaccines against the existing vaccines. As Claude went on to say, that’s because testing against a placebo in those cases would be unethical—you’d be knowingly exposing children to a dangerous, potentially deadly disease like measles—and is unnecessary because studies have already shown the original vaccine to be safe.Speaking of measles, that vaccine has been in the news a lot lately because the disease has returned to the United States after more than twenty years of “elimination” status, causing outbreaks and multiple deaths. The reason is falling vaccination rates. But Kennedy, rather than using his position to encourage vaccination, continues to suggest the shots may be dangerous.One supposed source of the danger is the clustering of three full shots (one each for measles, mumps, and rubella) into a single MMR shot. President Donald Trump has made a big deal about that, calling for the shots to be delivered separately, and Kennedy stood by that during an August CNN interview when he said “There is a recent study that just came out that supports President Trump on that. It looks at the timeline for when the autism epidemic began and . . . it’s a synthesis of—essentially a meta-review—of all the existing science. And it very strongly supports the president.”Claude’s verdict:After searching for references in the popular press—including from Factcheck.org, which has been doing heroic work scrutinizing Kennedy these past two years—Claude did its own literature search. It found no credible evidence to substantiate Kennedy’s statement, and instead concluded that “the recent published research points the other way.”The truth is rarely as tidy as we’d like it to be.That’s why we think journalism should be a process of discovery—not a daily exercise in confirming what everyone already believes.We follow the facts. We argue about what they mean. We learn from one another. We admit when we get things wrong. And, whenever possible, we have a little fun along the way.If that sounds like a community you’d like to be part of, come on in.Join Bulwark+ todayCLAUDE WAS CAREFUL TO NOTE—accurately—that Kennedy’s claims typically start with real facts or studies, which give them the veneer of credibility if you don’t know the context or understand the way he’s twisting the implications.One example of this chicanery is the way Kennedy talks about an earlier version of the polio vaccine, which was grown in monkey cells. A virus infected some of the cells that produced vaccines between 1955 and 1963. Here’s how Kennedy used that story during a 2023 podcast interview:The polio vaccine contained a virus called simian virus 40, SV40. It’s one of the most carcinogenic materials that is known to man. In fact, it’s used now by scientists around the world to induce tumors in rats and guinea pigs in labs. But it was in that vaccine—98 million people who got that vaccine, and my generation got it, and now you’ve had this explosion of soft tissue cancers in our generation that killed many, many, many, many more people than polio ever did.That claim has stuck with me because polio was such an awful disease, causing more than 3,000 deaths and many more cases of paralysis in 1952, the peak year before the vaccine’s 1955 introduction. The polio vaccine is in many ways the quintessential vaccine success story, and here Kennedy was suggesting that, rather than a medical miracle, the shot had been a nightmare.Except it was a miracle. Kennedy’s statement was “false,” according to Claude:Kennedy had botched some of the statistics and suggested a link between the virus and human cancer that studies have not established, Claude reported, though the AI interface told me the biggest problem with Kennedy’s argument was about the supposed “explosion” of cancers:The population data don’t show one. [The Institute of Medicine]’s summary: studies of people who received polio vaccine during 1955–1963 provide evidence of no increased cancer risk. A meta-analysis of five published studies did not support the idea that SV40 exposure increases overall cancer incidence or cancer mortality. [The National Cancer Institute] told Congress in 2003 that follow-up of vaccine recipients showed no excess of cancer, including a study of 1.8 million recipients of a widely contaminated Danish polio vaccine.But sometimes Kennedy’s distortions are less subtle, especially when it comes to the COVID-19 vaccines. Kennedy famously described them as “the deadliest ever made.” Claude judged that claim “false”:The source is the federal Vaccine Adverse Event Reporting System, or VAERS, through which people can report injuries and illnesses after vaccination. The CDC and the FDA use reports as possible safety signals, which they investigate, but absent evidence confirming the injuries—and linking them to vaccines—they don’t prove anything. As Claude noted, “The system’s own disclaimer says report counts can’t be used to draw conclusions about whether, how often, or how severely vaccines cause problems.”ShareDIFFERENT AI MODELS are trained differently, and can use different approaches to reasoning and problem-solving. So I tried another AI assistant, OpenAI’s ChatGPT. Here’s how it rated the four Kennedy claims:False / seriously misleading.Unsupported / misleading, and the characterization of the study is wrong.The first part is true; the central cancer claim is unsupported/false.False.Then I turned to Google’s Gemini. Here was its response:False / Highly InaccurateFalse / Unsupported by ScienceInaccurate and MisleadingFalse / Factually IncorrectFinally I went to Grok, Elon Musk’s AI assistant, and got this:False/inaccurateFalseMostly false/highly misleadingFalseYes, even Musk’s chatbot was reacting to Kennedy with the AI equivalent of AYFKM.I can’t say any of this surprised me. In reporting on Kennedy over the past year, I’ve read every reputable source I could find and spoken to at least a dozen different scientists about Kennedy’s claims. They have been unanimous in their opinion that Kennedy is not just wrong, but very, very wrong. But just to be sure, I checked with Emanuel too.“The great thing about using AI to check medical information,” he told me, “is that it shows RFK Jr. doesn’t know what he is talking about.”Want to comment? Join Bulwark+1Kennedy was citing something he said he had heard from OpenAI CEO Sam Altman.

articles.headline: Solos lets a wearer pick ChatGPT, Claude or Gemini, and AirGo 1.27.0 adds three languages - MIXED Reality News
articles.body: Solos lets a wearer pick ChatGPT, Claude or Gemini, and AirGo 1.27.0 adds three languages    MIXED Reality News

scored.body:
Solos shipped AirGo 1.27.0 on October 3 at 00:00 UTC, adding Romanian, Italian and Georgian and sharpening the live translation mode its glasses are sold on. The feature that separates Solos from the rest of the shelf is older and stranger: the wearer picks which assistant answers, from ChatGPT, Claude or Gemini, where a Ray-Ban Meta owner gets Meta AI and nothing else.

AirGo 1.27.0 reached the App Store on October 3 at 00:00 UTC. Image: Solos Image: Solos

The App Store listing says SolosChat 4.0 is "powered by leading multimodal LLMs including ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, and more" and offers "Support for multiple AI models to suit your needs", across the AirGo3, AirGo A5, AirGo V and AirGo V2 frames. Solos does not publish which version of any of the three it calls, and the choice is described only in its own marketing copy.

Three languages, and no total to go with them

The release notes say "Added Romanian, Italian, and Georgian language support" without naming the feature they belong to, and list "Improved latency and accuracy for Instant Translate" as a separate line. All three do turn up in the app's own App Store interface-language list, which now runs to 13 entries, read on October 3 at 21:35 UTC, and an interface language is not a translation language. Solos publishes no current total for its translator, so three were added and the sum is its own business.

Translation on these frames comes in two shapes, which Solos calls 1-to-1 Mode, "Perfect for face-to-face conversations", and Instant Translate Mode, "Continuous live translation and transcription". The rest of 1.27.0 is housekeeping: a default Bluetooth media volume setting, a larger maximum chat font, steadier Wi-Fi and photo syncing, and fixes for camera controls and capture status.

What the glasses themselves do

The AirGo V2 is the camera model, quoted at 16 MP stills and 2K video at 30 fps, with live streaming and voice commands in the form "Hey Solos, take a photo". Solos scopes those commands to the A5 and the V2. Whisper Messages reads incoming notifications through the temples, and Whisper Events speaks calendar reminders.

Prime 1 and Prime 2, the two AirGo V2 frames, are both listed at $299 on Solos' own store, which reports its prices in US dollars, read on October 3 at 21:35 UTC. Three accessories went up on September 29 in the same dollars: a ClearView Temple at $39, a Prime 2 Clip-On Bundle at $49 and a Prime 2 Privacy Kit at $79, the last of which Solos describes with a single line, "Framefront are not included".

Solos sells more than the two Prime frames. The AirGo A5 Hydro styles are $249 each with the Hydro 15 at $349, and the older AirGo V Krypton 2 is $299, all read at the same time. SolosChat 4.0 and the model picker cover all four generations, so the choice is not reserved for the camera frames.

The app itself is the oldest thing here, on the App Store since February 2020, and the translator long predates the model picker: the AirGo3 was up to 25 languages in 2024. A picker is a small thing to put in a settings screen and a large thing to keep, because it means Solos has to hold three providers steady at once while rivals ship firmware for one assistant.
