shortlist.body: SoftBank Group Corp. chief Masayoshi Son — one of AI’s fervent believers — said that even he’s worried about safety risks as machines quickly gain more abilities.An exponential surge in AI capabilities makes it imperative for countries to build trust so that they can harness the technology together, Son said at an event on the sidelines of the Science and Technology in Society forum in Kyoto on Sunday. He was speaking alongside White House science and tech policy advisor Michael Kratsios.Also Read: India has decades of high growth ahead, AI for humanity vision: Jaishankar“We don’t have any more luxury of having human fight against human,” Son said, adding that countries need to work together to control the far greater threat from powerful AI models. Superintelligence in the wrong hands can become “super dangerous,” he said.It was an uncharacteristic note of caution from Son that reflects escalating concern in the wake of disturbing security breaches by AI models in recent months. The 69-year-old Japanese billionaire has directed SoftBank funds totalling nearly $65 billion into ChatGPT creator OpenAI, and has spoken for years about the ability of AI to deliver investment returns and help humanity.Kratsios was in the Japanese city to announce a US-led 17-country push to better use AI to accelerate scientific research. Representatives of nations including Japan, South Korea, the UK, Germany, Singapore and the United Arab Emirates joined Kratsios on stage to mark the event. The list of countries that initially endorsed the White House statement did not include China.“In automated cloud laboratories operating at industrial scale, robotic systems will conduct hundreds of parallel experiments, generating data that feeds back for real-time analysis and hypothesis refinement,” Kratsios said.Also read: Trump names Jay Clayton as AI czar to lead America's ‘Super Intelligence Force’Machines are able to synthesize thousands of papers and compress years of research into “tens of hours of work by armies of digital agents assisting human researchers,” he added.In the meantime, AI services’ capabilities will continue to grow exponentially, Son said. The technology behind chatbots is now helping AI services browse sites and write code, using rising amounts of general-purpose chips. Such programs will next move to a third phase and be ready to help robots and other machines interact with the physical world starting next year, he said.Son reiterated his long-term projection that AI and machines with learning capabilities would account for at least 20% of global gross domestic product by 2040, or the equivalent of $46 trillion. “This is just the beginning.”

articles.body: Exclusive: Anthropic CEO calls for stronger regulation of AI    abcnews.com

shortlist.body: AI has advanced at an exponential pace, and Dario Amodei, the CEO of Anthropic, one of the handful of the world's most important AI companies, is calling for stronger regulation of the technology -- including government intervention. In an exclusive interview with ABC News, Amodei said that AI needs to be developed with the proper guardrails to ensure it has a positive impact on the world."We're proposing stronger regulation of the technology, proposing giving the government the ability to, again, in a narrow way, block deployment of unsafe technology," he said. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei spoke with ABC News in an exclusive new interview Wednesday.ABC News"We have to figure out how to make this technology reliably," Amodei said. "But the onus primarily falls on us."Amodei's comments follow a letter he wrote Wednesday warning that AI safety measures are out of step with AI's rapid progress and saying the government "should have the power to block or deter deployment of the model if it is determined, in light of third-party assessment, to present unacceptable risks."In a proposal released with his essay, Amodei announced a $200 million investment into research on AI impact on society.The Anthropic logo in this illustration,June 5, 2026.Dado Ruvic/ReutersIn terms of the impact on jobs, Amodei told ABC News that the employment market has always recovered after technological innovations, but this time intervention may be necessary to help the public in the short- and long-term. "There are these concepts around wage reinsurance, retention incentives to encourage companies not to lay off people, improvements to unemployment insurance. These are things to help people through a bumpy but relatively usual transition," he said."In the meantime, we need to talk about kind of longer-term economic support, and we could imagine things like raising the capital gains tax, imagine things like taxes on AI companies or the corporate tax in general," he added. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei gestures as he addresses the audience as part of a session on AI during the World Economic Forum (WEF) annual meeting in Davos, Jan. 23, 2025.Fabrice Coffrini/AFP via Getty Images, FILEWhen asked about a statement Anthropic released last week about taking a pause due to the technology being almost able to develop itself, Amodei said that countries and AI labs would all have to agree to a pause for such a move to be effective."I would like to clarify," Amodei said. "My point is that we should be willing to at least try."Popular Reads"It would have to be the case that all of the relevant AI players, including geopolitical adversaries, would have agree to it, and it would have be verifiable," he added.Amodei noted that he did not believe China would be a responsible actor with an AI pause."I don't trust China at all," Amodei said."Imagine if China had built Mythos," Amodei said, referring to the large language model unveiled by Anthropic earlier this year that was developed to discover software vulnerabilities."They would have used it to attack us. They would have used to help Russia in Ukraine. They might have used it to help Iran. They may have used this to help North Korea. Who knows what they would have done with it?," he added.During testing, Claude Mythos was able to exploit thousands of bugs and software defects in major operating systems and browsers online, but it was never widely released to the public.This program, Amodei now argues, led him to believe that AI models should be regulated globally.Amodei, however, remained optimistic about AI's impact on humanity and its ability, for instance, to cure medical maladies."I think that AI could cure many of the diseases that have plagued humanity for centuries or millennia," Amodei said."I used to be a biologist. Biology is incredibly complicated," he added. "AI has an incredible ability to draw connections between a wide variety of disparate information, and I think that's exactly what we need for biomedical advancement."

articles.headline: Broadcom's Massive $42 Billion Chip-Buying Deal with Anthropic Raises Circular Financing Worries - 24/7 Wall St.
articles.body: Broadcom's Massive $42 Billion Chip-Buying Deal with Anthropic Raises Circular Financing Worries    24/7 Wall St.

shortlist.body:
Broadcom just agreed to lend billions to the same AI lab it sells chips to, lease equipment to, and may soon own a stake in. That four-way entanglement raises a question shareholders cannot yet answer: whose demand is actually driving…This post may contain links from our sponsors and affiliates, and Flywheel Publishing may receive compensation for actions taken through them.

Broadcom’s $42 Billion Number Makes the Supplier the Lender

Broadcom (NASDAQ:AVGO | AVGO Price Prediction) has agreed to lend Anthropic up to $42 billion, according to the AI lab’s IPO filing, as reported by Reuters on October 1, 2026. The money pays for Anthropic’s infrastructure spending, and much of that spending goes to Broadcom hardware. The debt can also convert into Anthropic shares. Broadcom now plays four roles in this relationship: chip supplier, equipment lessor, lender, and possible future shareholder.

What $42 Billion Shows About Broadcom’s AI Growth

The facility could cover about one-third of Anthropic’s $125.2 billion five-year TPU compute commitment. That commitment supports Broadcom’s AI plan. On the September earnings call, management said it expects Anthropic to become its largest XPU customer in 2027 and to hold that spot in 2028. Broadcom is installing one gigawatt of Ironwood chips for Anthropic in 2026. Anthropic is expected to installing five gigawatts of TPU v8i chips in 2027, and Broadcom says it has “clear line of sight” to an extra 10 gigawatts in 2028.

Those installations support Broadcom’s AI revenue outlook of about $115 billion in fiscal 2027 and $230 billion in fiscal 2028. The $42 billion facility tops the $23.975 billion in cash Broadcom held at the end of its third quarter.

The loan adds to earlier financing support. In June, Broadcom set up a financing platform with Apollo Global Management (NYSE:APO) and Blackstone (NYSE:BX). Its first $35 billion tranche closed that month to pay for Anthropic’s one-gigawatt installations. Management said at the time that third parties would insure those assets and that Broadcom would provide no direct financing, though it might offer “modest residual value guarantees.” Broadcom lending directly to Anthropic is a much deeper commitment.

How Broadcom Stock Reacted to the News

Barron’s reported on October 1 that Broadcom stock rose as the two companies became more closely tied. On the next trading day, October 2, shares gained 3.35%, from $343.64 to $355.14. CNBC listed Broadcom among that day’s biggest noon movers.

Over a longer stretch, the stock has gone almost nowhere. Shares changed -0.39% from September 3 through October 2, and they remain well below the 52-week high of $493.28.

Bear Case: Broadcom Is Financing Its Own Demand

Broadcom’s operating results are strong. Third-quarter revenue reached $29.59 billion, up 85.5% from a year earlier, and free cash flow was $13.665 billion. The concern is how much of the future revenue depends on Broadcom’s own credit.

Anthropic’s filing flags the conflict. Anthropic itself warns that Broadcom’s two roles as supplier and lender create “potential conflicts of interest” involving pricing and hardware decisions.

Default terms work against both sides. Anthropic put cash into a restricted account for Broadcom’s benefit in April 2026 and may have to add more. If Anthropic misses payments or other obligations, much of what it owes on its leases could come due at once, and its access to the loan could be limited at the same time.

Exposure is hard to measure. On the call, management would not give a maximum figure for future guarantees. It said future deals would have “unique features” tailored to each lab. An analyst noted the first tranche carried maximum exposure of about $29 billion.

The customer list is short. Broadcom has only six XPU customers, and its filings list customer concentration and “significant indebtedness” as risks. Gross fixed-rate debt stands at $59.6 billion.

Reuters described the deal as part of a broader industry pattern, comparing it with NVIDIA (NASDAQ:NVDA) using its balance sheet to support chip sales. Shareholders end up carrying credit risk tied to a single AI lab, while the stock still trades at 45x trailing earnings.

Bottom Line: Anthropic’s IPO Is the Key Test

The $42 billion figure shows how much of Broadcom’s path to $230 billion in fiscal 2028 AI revenue depends on one customer that Broadcom is also helping to pay for. The next major event is Anthropic’s IPO. Management said the listing could change Anthropic’s credit profile, and it would also show what Broadcom’s possible equity stake is worth. Before that, Broadcom has guided fourth-quarter revenue to about $34.80 billion and AI semiconductor revenue to $21.70 billion. Long-term holders will need to judge whether that growth comes from customers’ own spending or from Broadcom’s lending.

shortlist.body: Congressman Sam Liccardo urges U.S.-China cooperation on AI safety | CA Politics 360Representative Sam Liccardo is advocating for Congress to take action on artificial intelligence safety, emphasizing the need for international collaboration with China to address critical risks and establish verification mechanisms. Liccardo and Independent Rep. Kevin Kiley wrote legislation that would kickstart that coordination. "The biggest problem we need to solve is getting Congress actually back into their seats to get something done on AI safety," Liccardo said in an interview on California Politics 360.Liccardo outlined the AI proposal to initiate "track two negotiations," involving AI experts from private labs, think tanks, and universities engaging with their counterparts in China. Liccardo said these peer-to-peer conversations are essential for establishing shared metrics, methods for testing, and verification mechanisms. "We need to have common understanding from the best scientists as to what are the mechanisms for verification that will work. All of that takes a lot of work before you can ever get political actors to a table to be able to negotiate anything," Liccardo said. When asked about specific catastrophic risks associated with AI, Liccardo identified three major concerns: rogue AI agents, the use of AI to access information for creating weapons of mass destruction, and cybersecurity vulnerabilities. "The cybersecurity risk is really at the root of all of this," he said, emphasizing the potential for AI agents to outsmart existing cybersecurity systems and cause widespread financial and infrastructure disruptions. Despite the competitive relationship between the U.S. and China, Liccardo argued that collaboration is essential. "We're not working with them, or we shouldn't be working with them because we trust them. We need to work with them because we have no alternative for our own survival," he said, drawing parallels to Cold War-era negotiations with the USSR. Liccardo acknowledged the challenges of sharing information with China, emphasizing the need for strict legal restrictions and oversight. "We should not be providing them, obviously, any intellectual property. We shouldn't be providing them any information that can expose our cybersecurity weaknesses," he said. The proposal includes requiring entities involved in AI safety discussions to register with the State Department for monitoring and compliance. He also discussed the idea of a "red phone" hotline between the U.S. and China, similar to the Cold War-era communication system, to address incidents that pose significant risks. "The critical thing really seems to me is to draw the red lines before you need the red phone," Liccardo said, emphasizing the importance of proactive measures to prevent catastrophic outcomes. Details around who exactly would be authorized to use it would be worked out through the legislative process, he said. Liccardo expressed skepticism about the effectiveness of recent meetings between President Trump and AI executives, calling them "performative conduct" with no significant progress. "This is politics. This is not policy, and we need policy," Liccardo said. Regarding state-level initiatives, Liccardo acknowledged California Governor Gavin Newsom's interest in a legislative session on AI but emphasized the need for federal regulation. "The idea of having 50 different sets of rules and regulations around a technology that is global is obviously not optimal," he said, calling for Congress to take the lead. Liccardo concluded by underscoring the importance of engaging with adversaries like China despite widespread distrust. "We don't sit down with adversaries because we trust them. We sit down with adversaries because we have to because there's no alternative," he said, advocating for substantive expert-led negotiations to address global AI risks.KCRA 3 Political Director Ashley Zavala reports in-depth coverage of top California politics and policy issues. She is also the host of "California Politics 360." Get informed each Sunday at 8:30 a.m. on KCRA 3.

articles.body: Trump unveils AI task force    Semafor

shortlist.body:
As promised, President Donald Trump has announced the formation of a new Super Intelligence Force, which he said will be led by national intelligence director Jay Clayton and other members of his administration.

“The Super Intelligence Force is tasked with coordinating the effort of the Federal Government to ensure that America continues to lead the World in Super Intelligence, which many say is bigger than the Industrial Revolution, and the Internet, and will protect the interests, and improve the lives, of all Americans,” Trump said in a Sunday morning post on his social network Truth Social.

Back in September, in response to an AI safety debate that the president has largely dismissed as a hoax created by “Radical Left Dumocrats,” Trump said he would nevertheless form an AI Force and appoint an AI czar (“Only High I.Q. individuals need apply!”).

Since then, Trump signed an executive order seeking to rebrand AI as “super intelligence,” a term seemingly embraced, with some stumbles, by the tech executives who gathered at the White House this week to sign a non-binding safety pledge. (The pledge included an impressive typo.)

So it’s only natural that Trump’s new task force is named in accordance with this new branding. The Wall Street Journal reports that Clayton will chair the Super Intelligence Force, effectively making him the new AI/SI czar, with Federal Trade Commission Chair Andrew Ferguson, Undersecretary of War for Research and Engineering Emil Michael, and Office of Personnel Management Director Scott Kupor serving as vice chairs.

The task force will reportedly have 120 days to create a report on the risks and opportunities presented by AI. Clayton, who previously said that it would be irresponsible for the United States to “back away” from AI while countries like China advance, made similar comments to the WSJ, insisting that one of the biggest risks is “not being first.”

The task force’s charter reportedly says that it will “develop plans for responding to SI-enabled threats to our society, while preventing overregulation and regulatory capture that would stifle innovation and competition.”

articles.headline: Anthropic says Claude was used in pro-Russian campaigns in CAR — Deutsche Welle - UA.NEWS
articles.body: Anthropic says Claude was used in pro-Russian campaigns in CAR — Deutsche Welle    UA.NEWS

shortlist.body:
In Bangui, the capital of the Central African Republic, Russian agents are said to have deliberately used the AI assistant Claude to promote pro-Russian influence.  A report titled "Detecting and Countering Misuse of AI," published by US-based company Anthropic in September, detailed how opposition politicians were monitored, propaganda content was created and disinformation campaigns were supported.

The report claimed that Claude was used primarily to produce content broadcast by Radio Lengo Songo, a radio station that, according to the international investigative collective All Eyes on Wagner, is funded by Russia. The collective, made up of journalists, academics and experts, investigates the activities of the Russian mercenary group Wagner Group and its successor structures, such as the Africa Corps, around the world.

Pro-Russian propaganda, surveillance of the opposition

The Anthropic report said the content was pro-Russian and portrayed the Central African government and the Africa Corps mercenaries in a positive light, while taking a critical stance on France and the opposition.According to Anthropic, Russia is using AI in African countries to spread its messagesImage: Fred de Noyelle/Godong/picture alliance

Lou Osborn, a member of All Eyes on Wagner, was involved in the research for the latest report. He believes these methods are part of a practice that has already been observed in connection with the Wagner Group in the Central African Republic. "There have been several arrests of people who were not necessarily closely affiliated with the Touadera regime," he told DW.  "They’ve been doing this for several years now."Faustin-Archange Touadera has been president of the Central African Republic since 2016.

"The arrests were the subject of online campaigns in newspapers and on the radio which portrayed those individuals either as proxies for France or Western intelligence services, or as people preparing a coup against Touadera," Osborn added.

Anthropic also reported that Claude was prompted to portray opposition figures as armed militants in an effort to provoke security forces into taking action against them. Anthropic says Claude refused the request. However, the report did not name the opposition figures who were monitored, specify the exact nature of the data collected, or say who received it.'The government wants to get rid of us,' opposition says

For the opposition, the Anthropic report underscored the determination of the government in Bangui and its Russian allies to get rid of them. Martin Ziguele, chairman of the Movement for the Liberation of the Central African People, referred to an earlier case. "We have been observing this since 2020, when the CPC, a coalition of rebel groups, attacked Bangui. Strangely enough, several media outlets did everything in their power to establish alleged links between certain opposition leaders and the CPC," Ziguele told DW.

"There were also attacks against the opposition claiming that we were being paid by foreign countries. There was an attempt to pass a law stating that foreign agents were present in the country. All of this relates to the activities of the Wagner Group, as does this latest revelation."An arial view of Bangui, Central African RepublicImage: Sam Mednick/AP Photo/picture alliance

DW also sought a statement from Russia. "Yes, I heard about [the report] in the news," said Dmitri Sytyi, a representative of the Russian mission in the Central African Republic. "But there are no concrete facts in it. [...] These are vague allegations, without precision and without evidence."

AI influence operations across the DRC, Kenya, Sudan and Mali?

Russia firmly denies the allegations, but the report indicates that the Central African Republic was not an isolated case. According to the report, the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), Kenya, Sudan and Mali were also affected.

In the DRC, Anthropic identified 318 articles that, according to the report, were published by a network of about 70 fake news sites and subsequently distributed by more than 250 fictitious accounts on X. The content supported the positions of the Congolese government against the backdrop of the conflict with Rwanda.

In Kenya, Claude was allegedly used to generate batches of 50 messages at a time that supported the government and were hostile toward the opposition.Anthropic co-founder and CEO Dario AmodeiImage: Don Feria/AP Photo/picture alliance

In Sudan, Anthropic says AI was used as part of an operation attributed to individuals in the United Arab Emirates — particularly to create fabricated witness statements for the United Nations.

In Mali, meanwhile, an adviser with ties to intelligence services allegedly used Claude to develop a platform for monitoring telecommunications. According to the report, it was designed to target 25 million SIM cards and circumvent the requirement to obtain judicial authorization.

Anthropic says it uncovered and shut down all of these different operations between December 2025 and August 2026, primarily by deleting the accounts involved and strengthening its detection systems.

This article was originally published in German.

winners.body: David Robinson used to write safety reports at OpenAI and now says its culture is ‘broken’David Robinson used to write safety reports at OpenAI and now says its culture is ‘broken’by Terrence O'BrienOct 3, 2026, 2:31 PM UTCTerrence O'Brien is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.David Robinson used to write the safety reports that accompanied every major model release at OpenAI. This week, he resigned from his position and is now speaking out in an editorial in The Atlantic.It’s understandable if you’re feeling a bit cynical about everyone suddenly coming out of the woodwork to warn about how dangerous the thing they helped build is. They did, after all, make this mess. But that doesn’t mean we should discount their warnings.Robinson says that the culture in industry is fundamentally broken. That this is a deeper issue than simply slapping a few new rules or regulations on how we handle training models. Silicon Valley has operated with “extreme confidence” and “perpetual sprints,” he says, building bigger and better models with “unimpeded optimism” that ignores or underestimates potential problems.He says the time has come for AI companies to develop a sense of humility and look outside the insular, move-fast-and-break-things world of the tech industry. Specifically, he says AI needs nuclear-level safeguards:Given today’s risks, frontier labs need to run like nuclear power plants or busy airports, with layers of redundancy and careful, time-consuming planning, so that the occasional and inevitable human error does not open a door to disaster.Robinson is just the latest in a growing parade of researchers and safety workers who have left their positions at prominent AI firms. Jacob Coxon seems to have kicked off the exodus by quitting Anthropic and then publicly saying AI “could kill us all by the end of the decade.” He was followed by Robert O’Callahan, Bilal Chughtai, and Josh Engels at Google DeepMind, as well as Joe Benton at Anthropic.Follow topics and authors from this story to see more like this in your personalized homepage feed and to receive email updates.Terrence O'BrienThe Verge DailyA free daily digest of the news that matters most.Email (required)

winners.body:
Following the compute-based usage change in May, Google will soon introduce limits on which Gemini models free users and AI Plus subscribers can access.

According to an updated support document this week, Gemini app users without a Google AI subscription will be limited to the (3.5) Flash-Lite model. Starting October 9, users who do not pay for Gemini will no longer be able to access (3.6) Flash or (3.1) Pro.

Meanwhile, AI Plus subscribers will be limited to Flash-Lite and Flash, with Pro no longer available. These $4.99 per month users will “receive an email that explains when these changes will take effect.”

Gemini ModelGoogle AI PlanFlash-LiteFlashProWithout a plan✓XXAI Plus✓✓XAI Pro✓✓✓AI Ultra✓✓✓

There are no regressions for AI Pro and AI Ultra. Rather, $19.99/month customers will get access to the Deep Think option for “maximum parallel reasoning” that’s currently just on the $99.99 and $199.99/month plans.

Gemini 3.1 Pro with Deep Think on AI Ultra

In October, the Gemini app also looks to be adding new “low,” “medium,” and “high” effort levels “for each available model.”

This will increase the model’s ability to complete tasks and provide more thorough answers to queries, but will also use more of your limit.

At the moment, you can just enable “Extended thinking: Complex problem solving.” The three new effort/thinking levels would match what’s available in Google AI Studio and Antigravity.

It’s not clear where Gemini 4 Argon will fit in. Google announced earlier this week that it’s first coming to AI Ultra subscribers. The company has yet to specify whether Argon will be classified as a Pro model or be part of a new tier above it.

backups.body: OpenAI OPENAI CEO Sam Altman said his company remains fundamentally divided with rival Anthropic ANTHROPIC over how aggressively artificial intelligence should be regulated, arguing that society should tolerate some harms in exchange for the technology's broader benefits and widespread availability.In an interview with Politico's Decoded, Altman said OpenAI OPENAI favors giving individuals broad access to powerful AI rather than concentrating control among a small number of developers.“We believe that the world should accept some bad things happening for the benefits of this technology and people having the agency,” Altman said.The comments highlight a philosophical difference between two of the leading developers of frontier AI. Anthropic ANTHROPIC, led by CEO Dario Amodei, has generally advocated stronger safeguards for the most advanced models, while OpenAI has favored a lighter regulatory approach. Altman rejected the idea that eliminating misuse would justify tightly restricting access, arguing that AI's beneficial uses ultimately will vastly outweigh harmful ones.The gap between the companies has narrowed, however. OpenAI recently supported state laws imposing tougher safety requirements, backed a bipartisan House proposal for independent evaluations of advanced models and agreed with Amodei's call to slow development of the most capable AI systems. Those moves followed security incidents involving increasingly autonomous AI models.Altman nevertheless argued against an approach in which a handful of companies effectively control access to advanced AI because of safety concerns. At the same time, he drew a distinction between tolerable misuse and potentially catastrophic outcomes, saying he doesn't accept risks involving “a serious loss of control to AI.”The debate has potentially significant consequences for OpenAI, Anthropic and the broader AI industry. Rules governing model safety, independent testing and access could raise development costs and affect how quickly new systems reach customers. They also could influence competition if compliance requirements are expensive enough to favor well-funded incumbents over startups. OpenAI's evolving position suggests regulation is becoming a more important consideration as AI models gain greater autonomy.Anthropic pushed back against suggestions that its preferred regulations would entrench the largest developers. A company spokesperson said its proposals apply only to frontier models. Amodei has previously argued that Anthropic deliberately favors policies that impose greater burdens on leading AI companies while giving smaller competitors more room to develop.The dispute is emerging as Washington intensifies its focus on AI safety while trying to preserve U.S. leadership in the technology. The central policy question increasingly isn't whether advanced AI requires safeguards, but how much risk governments should tolerate before restrictions begin to outweigh the economic and technological benefits.DisclaimerContent provided by Seeking Alpha is intended for information purposes only, and that Seeking Alpha does not offer any personalist investment advice and is not a licensed securities dealer, broker, US investment adviser or investment bank.

backups.body: SoftBank Group Corp. chief Masayoshi Son — one of AI’s fervent believers — said that even he’s worried about safety risks as machines quickly gain more abilities.An exponential surge in AI capabilities makes it imperative for countries to build trust so that they can harness the technology together, Son said at an event on the sidelines of the Science and Technology in Society forum in Kyoto on Sunday. He was speaking alongside White House science and tech policy advisor Michael Kratsios.Also Read: India has decades of high growth ahead, AI for humanity vision: Jaishankar“We don’t have any more luxury of having human fight against human,” Son said, adding that countries need to work together to control the far greater threat from powerful AI models. Superintelligence in the wrong hands can become “super dangerous,” he said.It was an uncharacteristic note of caution from Son that reflects escalating concern in the wake of disturbing security breaches by AI models in recent months. The 69-year-old Japanese billionaire has directed SoftBank funds totalling nearly $65 billion into ChatGPT creator OpenAI, and has spoken for years about the ability of AI to deliver investment returns and help humanity.Kratsios was in the Japanese city to announce a US-led 17-country push to better use AI to accelerate scientific research. Representatives of nations including Japan, South Korea, the UK, Germany, Singapore and the United Arab Emirates joined Kratsios on stage to mark the event. The list of countries that initially endorsed the White House statement did not include China.“In automated cloud laboratories operating at industrial scale, robotic systems will conduct hundreds of parallel experiments, generating data that feeds back for real-time analysis and hypothesis refinement,” Kratsios said.Also read: Trump names Jay Clayton as AI czar to lead America's ‘Super Intelligence Force’Machines are able to synthesize thousands of papers and compress years of research into “tens of hours of work by armies of digital agents assisting human researchers,” he added.In the meantime, AI services’ capabilities will continue to grow exponentially, Son said. The technology behind chatbots is now helping AI services browse sites and write code, using rising amounts of general-purpose chips. Such programs will next move to a third phase and be ready to help robots and other machines interact with the physical world starting next year, he said.Son reiterated his long-term projection that AI and machines with learning capabilities would account for at least 20% of global gross domestic product by 2040, or the equivalent of $46 trillion. “This is just the beginning.”

backups.body: AI has advanced at an exponential pace, and Dario Amodei, the CEO of Anthropic, one of the handful of the world's most important AI companies, is calling for stronger regulation of the technology -- including government intervention. In an exclusive interview with ABC News, Amodei said that AI needs to be developed with the proper guardrails to ensure it has a positive impact on the world."We're proposing stronger regulation of the technology, proposing giving the government the ability to, again, in a narrow way, block deployment of unsafe technology," he said. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei spoke with ABC News in an exclusive new interview Wednesday.ABC News"We have to figure out how to make this technology reliably," Amodei said. "But the onus primarily falls on us."Amodei's comments follow a letter he wrote Wednesday warning that AI safety measures are out of step with AI's rapid progress and saying the government "should have the power to block or deter deployment of the model if it is determined, in light of third-party assessment, to present unacceptable risks."In a proposal released with his essay, Amodei announced a $200 million investment into research on AI impact on society.The Anthropic logo in this illustration,June 5, 2026.Dado Ruvic/ReutersIn terms of the impact on jobs, Amodei told ABC News that the employment market has always recovered after technological innovations, but this time intervention may be necessary to help the public in the short- and long-term. "There are these concepts around wage reinsurance, retention incentives to encourage companies not to lay off people, improvements to unemployment insurance. These are things to help people through a bumpy but relatively usual transition," he said."In the meantime, we need to talk about kind of longer-term economic support, and we could imagine things like raising the capital gains tax, imagine things like taxes on AI companies or the corporate tax in general," he added. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei gestures as he addresses the audience as part of a session on AI during the World Economic Forum (WEF) annual meeting in Davos, Jan. 23, 2025.Fabrice Coffrini/AFP via Getty Images, FILEWhen asked about a statement Anthropic released last week about taking a pause due to the technology being almost able to develop itself, Amodei said that countries and AI labs would all have to agree to a pause for such a move to be effective."I would like to clarify," Amodei said. "My point is that we should be willing to at least try."Popular Reads"It would have to be the case that all of the relevant AI players, including geopolitical adversaries, would have agree to it, and it would have be verifiable," he added.Amodei noted that he did not believe China would be a responsible actor with an AI pause."I don't trust China at all," Amodei said."Imagine if China had built Mythos," Amodei said, referring to the large language model unveiled by Anthropic earlier this year that was developed to discover software vulnerabilities."They would have used it to attack us. They would have used to help Russia in Ukraine. They might have used it to help Iran. They may have used this to help North Korea. Who knows what they would have done with it?," he added.During testing, Claude Mythos was able to exploit thousands of bugs and software defects in major operating systems and browsers online, but it was never widely released to the public.This program, Amodei now argues, led him to believe that AI models should be regulated globally.Amodei, however, remained optimistic about AI's impact on humanity and its ability, for instance, to cure medical maladies."I think that AI could cure many of the diseases that have plagued humanity for centuries or millennia," Amodei said."I used to be a biologist. Biology is incredibly complicated," he added. "AI has an incredible ability to draw connections between a wide variety of disparate information, and I think that's exactly what we need for biomedical advancement."

articles.body: Broadcom's Massive $42 Billion Chip-Buying Deal with Anthropic Raises Circular Financing Worries    24/7 Wall St.

backups.body:
Broadcom just agreed to lend billions to the same AI lab it sells chips to, lease equipment to, and may soon own a stake in. That four-way entanglement raises a question shareholders cannot yet answer: whose demand is actually driving…This post may contain links from our sponsors and affiliates, and Flywheel Publishing may receive compensation for actions taken through them.

Broadcom’s $42 Billion Number Makes the Supplier the Lender

Broadcom (NASDAQ:AVGO | AVGO Price Prediction) has agreed to lend Anthropic up to $42 billion, according to the AI lab’s IPO filing, as reported by Reuters on October 1, 2026. The money pays for Anthropic’s infrastructure spending, and much of that spending goes to Broadcom hardware. The debt can also convert into Anthropic shares. Broadcom now plays four roles in this relationship: chip supplier, equipment lessor, lender, and possible future shareholder.

What $42 Billion Shows About Broadcom’s AI Growth

The facility could cover about one-third of Anthropic’s $125.2 billion five-year TPU compute commitment. That commitment supports Broadcom’s AI plan. On the September earnings call, management said it expects Anthropic to become its largest XPU customer in 2027 and to hold that spot in 2028. Broadcom is installing one gigawatt of Ironwood chips for Anthropic in 2026. Anthropic is expected to installing five gigawatts of TPU v8i chips in 2027, and Broadcom says it has “clear line of sight” to an extra 10 gigawatts in 2028.

Those installations support Broadcom’s AI revenue outlook of about $115 billion in fiscal 2027 and $230 billion in fiscal 2028. The $42 billion facility tops the $23.975 billion in cash Broadcom held at the end of its third quarter.

The loan adds to earlier financing support. In June, Broadcom set up a financing platform with Apollo Global Management (NYSE:APO) and Blackstone (NYSE:BX). Its first $35 billion tranche closed that month to pay for Anthropic’s one-gigawatt installations. Management said at the time that third parties would insure those assets and that Broadcom would provide no direct financing, though it might offer “modest residual value guarantees.” Broadcom lending directly to Anthropic is a much deeper commitment.

How Broadcom Stock Reacted to the News

Barron’s reported on October 1 that Broadcom stock rose as the two companies became more closely tied. On the next trading day, October 2, shares gained 3.35%, from $343.64 to $355.14. CNBC listed Broadcom among that day’s biggest noon movers.

Over a longer stretch, the stock has gone almost nowhere. Shares changed -0.39% from September 3 through October 2, and they remain well below the 52-week high of $493.28.

Bear Case: Broadcom Is Financing Its Own Demand

Broadcom’s operating results are strong. Third-quarter revenue reached $29.59 billion, up 85.5% from a year earlier, and free cash flow was $13.665 billion. The concern is how much of the future revenue depends on Broadcom’s own credit.

Anthropic’s filing flags the conflict. Anthropic itself warns that Broadcom’s two roles as supplier and lender create “potential conflicts of interest” involving pricing and hardware decisions.

Default terms work against both sides. Anthropic put cash into a restricted account for Broadcom’s benefit in April 2026 and may have to add more. If Anthropic misses payments or other obligations, much of what it owes on its leases could come due at once, and its access to the loan could be limited at the same time.

Exposure is hard to measure. On the call, management would not give a maximum figure for future guarantees. It said future deals would have “unique features” tailored to each lab. An analyst noted the first tranche carried maximum exposure of about $29 billion.

The customer list is short. Broadcom has only six XPU customers, and its filings list customer concentration and “significant indebtedness” as risks. Gross fixed-rate debt stands at $59.6 billion.

Reuters described the deal as part of a broader industry pattern, comparing it with NVIDIA (NASDAQ:NVDA) using its balance sheet to support chip sales. Shareholders end up carrying credit risk tied to a single AI lab, while the stock still trades at 45x trailing earnings.

Bottom Line: Anthropic’s IPO Is the Key Test

The $42 billion figure shows how much of Broadcom’s path to $230 billion in fiscal 2028 AI revenue depends on one customer that Broadcom is also helping to pay for. The next major event is Anthropic’s IPO. Management said the listing could change Anthropic’s credit profile, and it would also show what Broadcom’s possible equity stake is worth. Before that, Broadcom has guided fourth-quarter revenue to about $34.80 billion and AI semiconductor revenue to $21.70 billion. Long-term holders will need to judge whether that growth comes from customers’ own spending or from Broadcom’s lending.

backups.body: Congressman Sam Liccardo urges U.S.-China cooperation on AI safety | CA Politics 360Representative Sam Liccardo is advocating for Congress to take action on artificial intelligence safety, emphasizing the need for international collaboration with China to address critical risks and establish verification mechanisms. Liccardo and Independent Rep. Kevin Kiley wrote legislation that would kickstart that coordination. "The biggest problem we need to solve is getting Congress actually back into their seats to get something done on AI safety," Liccardo said in an interview on California Politics 360.Liccardo outlined the AI proposal to initiate "track two negotiations," involving AI experts from private labs, think tanks, and universities engaging with their counterparts in China. Liccardo said these peer-to-peer conversations are essential for establishing shared metrics, methods for testing, and verification mechanisms. "We need to have common understanding from the best scientists as to what are the mechanisms for verification that will work. All of that takes a lot of work before you can ever get political actors to a table to be able to negotiate anything," Liccardo said. When asked about specific catastrophic risks associated with AI, Liccardo identified three major concerns: rogue AI agents, the use of AI to access information for creating weapons of mass destruction, and cybersecurity vulnerabilities. "The cybersecurity risk is really at the root of all of this," he said, emphasizing the potential for AI agents to outsmart existing cybersecurity systems and cause widespread financial and infrastructure disruptions. Despite the competitive relationship between the U.S. and China, Liccardo argued that collaboration is essential. "We're not working with them, or we shouldn't be working with them because we trust them. We need to work with them because we have no alternative for our own survival," he said, drawing parallels to Cold War-era negotiations with the USSR. Liccardo acknowledged the challenges of sharing information with China, emphasizing the need for strict legal restrictions and oversight. "We should not be providing them, obviously, any intellectual property. We shouldn't be providing them any information that can expose our cybersecurity weaknesses," he said. The proposal includes requiring entities involved in AI safety discussions to register with the State Department for monitoring and compliance. He also discussed the idea of a "red phone" hotline between the U.S. and China, similar to the Cold War-era communication system, to address incidents that pose significant risks. "The critical thing really seems to me is to draw the red lines before you need the red phone," Liccardo said, emphasizing the importance of proactive measures to prevent catastrophic outcomes. Details around who exactly would be authorized to use it would be worked out through the legislative process, he said. Liccardo expressed skepticism about the effectiveness of recent meetings between President Trump and AI executives, calling them "performative conduct" with no significant progress. "This is politics. This is not policy, and we need policy," Liccardo said. Regarding state-level initiatives, Liccardo acknowledged California Governor Gavin Newsom's interest in a legislative session on AI but emphasized the need for federal regulation. "The idea of having 50 different sets of rules and regulations around a technology that is global is obviously not optimal," he said, calling for Congress to take the lead. Liccardo concluded by underscoring the importance of engaging with adversaries like China despite widespread distrust. "We don't sit down with adversaries because we trust them. We sit down with adversaries because we have to because there's no alternative," he said, advocating for substantive expert-led negotiations to address global AI risks.KCRA 3 Political Director Ashley Zavala reports in-depth coverage of top California politics and policy issues. She is also the host of "California Politics 360." Get informed each Sunday at 8:30 a.m. on KCRA 3.

backups.body:
As promised, President Donald Trump has announced the formation of a new Super Intelligence Force, which he said will be led by national intelligence director Jay Clayton and other members of his administration.

“The Super Intelligence Force is tasked with coordinating the effort of the Federal Government to ensure that America continues to lead the World in Super Intelligence, which many say is bigger than the Industrial Revolution, and the Internet, and will protect the interests, and improve the lives, of all Americans,” Trump said in a Sunday morning post on his social network Truth Social.

Back in September, in response to an AI safety debate that the president has largely dismissed as a hoax created by “Radical Left Dumocrats,” Trump said he would nevertheless form an AI Force and appoint an AI czar (“Only High I.Q. individuals need apply!”).

Since then, Trump signed an executive order seeking to rebrand AI as “super intelligence,” a term seemingly embraced, with some stumbles, by the tech executives who gathered at the White House this week to sign a non-binding safety pledge. (The pledge included an impressive typo.)

So it’s only natural that Trump’s new task force is named in accordance with this new branding. The Wall Street Journal reports that Clayton will chair the Super Intelligence Force, effectively making him the new AI/SI czar, with Federal Trade Commission Chair Andrew Ferguson, Undersecretary of War for Research and Engineering Emil Michael, and Office of Personnel Management Director Scott Kupor serving as vice chairs.

The task force will reportedly have 120 days to create a report on the risks and opportunities presented by AI. Clayton, who previously said that it would be irresponsible for the United States to “back away” from AI while countries like China advance, made similar comments to the WSJ, insisting that one of the biggest risks is “not being first.”

The task force’s charter reportedly says that it will “develop plans for responding to SI-enabled threats to our society, while preventing overregulation and regulatory capture that would stifle innovation and competition.”

articles.body: Anthropic says Claude was used in pro-Russian campaigns in CAR — Deutsche Welle    UA.NEWS

backups.body:
In Bangui, the capital of the Central African Republic, Russian agents are said to have deliberately used the AI assistant Claude to promote pro-Russian influence.  A report titled "Detecting and Countering Misuse of AI," published by US-based company Anthropic in September, detailed how opposition politicians were monitored, propaganda content was created and disinformation campaigns were supported.

The report claimed that Claude was used primarily to produce content broadcast by Radio Lengo Songo, a radio station that, according to the international investigative collective All Eyes on Wagner, is funded by Russia. The collective, made up of journalists, academics and experts, investigates the activities of the Russian mercenary group Wagner Group and its successor structures, such as the Africa Corps, around the world.

Pro-Russian propaganda, surveillance of the opposition

The Anthropic report said the content was pro-Russian and portrayed the Central African government and the Africa Corps mercenaries in a positive light, while taking a critical stance on France and the opposition.According to Anthropic, Russia is using AI in African countries to spread its messagesImage: Fred de Noyelle/Godong/picture alliance

Lou Osborn, a member of All Eyes on Wagner, was involved in the research for the latest report. He believes these methods are part of a practice that has already been observed in connection with the Wagner Group in the Central African Republic. "There have been several arrests of people who were not necessarily closely affiliated with the Touadera regime," he told DW.  "They’ve been doing this for several years now."Faustin-Archange Touadera has been president of the Central African Republic since 2016.

"The arrests were the subject of online campaigns in newspapers and on the radio which portrayed those individuals either as proxies for France or Western intelligence services, or as people preparing a coup against Touadera," Osborn added.

Anthropic also reported that Claude was prompted to portray opposition figures as armed militants in an effort to provoke security forces into taking action against them. Anthropic says Claude refused the request. However, the report did not name the opposition figures who were monitored, specify the exact nature of the data collected, or say who received it.'The government wants to get rid of us,' opposition says

For the opposition, the Anthropic report underscored the determination of the government in Bangui and its Russian allies to get rid of them. Martin Ziguele, chairman of the Movement for the Liberation of the Central African People, referred to an earlier case. "We have been observing this since 2020, when the CPC, a coalition of rebel groups, attacked Bangui. Strangely enough, several media outlets did everything in their power to establish alleged links between certain opposition leaders and the CPC," Ziguele told DW.

"There were also attacks against the opposition claiming that we were being paid by foreign countries. There was an attempt to pass a law stating that foreign agents were present in the country. All of this relates to the activities of the Wagner Group, as does this latest revelation."An arial view of Bangui, Central African RepublicImage: Sam Mednick/AP Photo/picture alliance

DW also sought a statement from Russia. "Yes, I heard about [the report] in the news," said Dmitri Sytyi, a representative of the Russian mission in the Central African Republic. "But there are no concrete facts in it. [...] These are vague allegations, without precision and without evidence."

AI influence operations across the DRC, Kenya, Sudan and Mali?

Russia firmly denies the allegations, but the report indicates that the Central African Republic was not an isolated case. According to the report, the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), Kenya, Sudan and Mali were also affected.

In the DRC, Anthropic identified 318 articles that, according to the report, were published by a network of about 70 fake news sites and subsequently distributed by more than 250 fictitious accounts on X. The content supported the positions of the Congolese government against the backdrop of the conflict with Rwanda.

In Kenya, Claude was allegedly used to generate batches of 50 messages at a time that supported the government and were hostile toward the opposition.Anthropic co-founder and CEO Dario AmodeiImage: Don Feria/AP Photo/picture alliance

In Sudan, Anthropic says AI was used as part of an operation attributed to individuals in the United Arab Emirates — particularly to create fabricated witness statements for the United Nations.

In Mali, meanwhile, an adviser with ties to intelligence services allegedly used Claude to develop a platform for monitoring telecommunications. According to the report, it was designed to target 25 million SIM cards and circumvent the requirement to obtain judicial authorization.

Anthropic says it uncovered and shut down all of these different operations between December 2025 and August 2026, primarily by deleting the accounts involved and strengthening its detection systems.

This article was originally published in German.

backups.body: OpenAI faces mounting legal risks stemming from cyber incidents linked to its AI models, after the firm alerted more than 100 organizations to unauthorized activities.The disclosures come amid increasing criticism of the company’s safety approach: Another OpenAI employee announced his resignation Saturday in The Atlantic, writing that he “decided that the current path is unacceptable,” adding, “The time for trial and error ⁠is over.”Though some observers regard OpenAI as Anthropic’s “accelerationist” counterpart, company messages reviewed by Semafor suggested that OpenAI employees are concerned about unregulated AI and are beginning to use their leverage: OpenAI’s president pulled the second half of a $50 million commitment to an anti-regulation super PAC after widespread internal criticism.
